maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FUEL EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: Mr. CONMEE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 101) to amend the Electricity and Fuel Exportation Act. He said: In introducing this Bill, I desire to make a few explanations. The object of the Bill is to amend chapter 16 of the Act to Regulate the Exportation of Electrical power and certain liquids and gases. That Act was passed in 1907, and it provides for the export of certain quantities of electrical power or energy in cases where there is a surplus over the quantity that may be used in Canada. The purpose of the amendment is to make that. Act a little more specific. In the Act as

*2256
it now stands the word ' power * is defined by subsection (d), as follows:-
' Power ' means electrical power or energy produced in Canada.
Then,
' Fluid ' means petroleum, natural gas, water or other fluid, whether liquid or gaseous capable of being exported by means of pipe lines or other like contrivances and produced in Canada.
Then the Act provides that no person shall export 'electrical power or fluid without a license, and prescribes the conditions under which licenses are to be granted. Subsection 2 of section 3 provides that:
No person shall, without a license, construct or place in position any line or wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.
The word ' power ' in this case is used in this section of the Act, and is not accompanied by the word 'electrical/ as in subsection (d). In the definition of the word ' power ' it is stated that power means electrical power, or energy, produced in Canada, while in this section power is referred to without any reference to electricity. Then, by subsection 4, and especially by subsection 5, the conditions upon which power is to be granted are set up. I may say that cases have arisen in which there has been some little difficulty in administering the Act. In one case that I have knowledge of the company claimed that they were not entitled to provide power. Power, as generally defined by that word ' mechanical,' means mechanical, or hydraulic power, the power of the water wheel, and they held they were not bound to furnish any power of that kind, but that it must be electrical energy or none at all. I assume that the intention in passing this Act in 1907 was to provide for, first, the use of power so far as power was required by Canadian consumers, whether that power was in the form of mechanical power or electrical energy. I assume the intention was that Canadian users should be first supplied, and that then any surplus remaining over and above the Canadian'demand might be exported. The object of the amendments are to make that plain. For that purpose I propose to amend section 1 of the Act, chapter 16, by repealing that section and substituting a new section in lieu of it to this effect:-
This Act may be cited as the Power, Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
The difference is that in the present Bill it is stated:-
'This Act may be cited as the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.'

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FUEL EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I introduce the word ' power ' there so that it may be carried on through the different sections of the Act. Then I propose to repeal paragraph (b) of section 2 of the said Act and to substitute the following :-
Power means and includes mechanical or hydraulic power and electrical power or energy produced in Canada.
The only difference is that the words ' mechanical power ' are introduced in that section. Thep, section 3 provides for the export of power and fixes the conditions, and subsection 3, as it stands in the Act, reads:-
No person shall without a license construct or place in position any line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or any pipe line or any like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.
It is proposed to amend that section in this way:-
No person shall without a license construct or place in position any line of wire, cable or other .means of transmitting power or any conductor for the exportation of power or electrical energy.
The difference between the two is that the word ' cable ' is introduced in the amendment, and for the reason that power can be transmitted otherwise than by electrical energy. I know a case where power has been transmitted by cable for mining purposes a distance of one mile and a quarter, and it is, therefore, necessary to provide that such a contingency shall fall under the regulations of this Bill the same as if it were transmitted by wire. Subsection 5 of the Bill deals with the question of supplying power in Canada, and it reads:-
Any . such license may provide that the quantity of power or fluid to be exported shall be limited to the surplus after the licensee has supplied for distribution to the consumer for use in Canada power or fluid to the extent defined by such license at prices and in accordance with the conditions, rules and regulations provided by the Governor in Council.
That is the section under which the difficulty to which I alluded a moment ago arises. The company in the case I speak of claim that the word ' power ' used in this section does not mean hydraulic, or mechanical power, but that it referred to electrical power, and no other. Now, in amending the section, the language I am suggesting is as follows, which I propose in substitution:-
Any such license shall provide that the quantity of power or fluid to be exported shall be limited to the surplus after the licensee has from time to time, as in this Act provided, supplied power or fluid, and has also provided all proper or necessary means of supplying such power or fluid for use by consumers in Canada to the extent defined by such license.

I think that amendment is very necessary, and I believe it will make the Bill much more workable, for the reason that the provision that power has to be supplied to Canadian consumers does not appear to go far enough. The Bill, as it stands, provides that prices may 'be regulated by the license, but in this it goes further and provides that the conditions and means by which the power shall be furnished shall be provided by the license. The power is no use to the Canadian consumer if he cannot get it. For instance, ir. the case to which I refer, where the power was locked up in the power house, and the door barred, and the Canadian consumer could not get it, it would not be of any value even if a price were fixed as he could iiot Use it, and tlhe purpose of the Act was defeated. The question of the means and methods of using as well as to distributing power is just as important as the question of the power itself. I think every one will agree that it must have been the intention in drafting this Act and providing that the power should be supplied, that reasonable means should be employed for supplying it. That being so, I think the Act should be more definite, and should stipulate with regard to these matters.

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FUEL EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman explain in what form is hydraulic power transmitted?

maintopic: ELECTRICITY AND FUEL EXPORTATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is transmitted by cable for considerable distances. There may be other means of transmitting it, but in my own experience I have dealt with power which was transmitted three-quarters of a mile by cable, and I know a case where it was transmitted one mile and a quarter, and I see no reason why it should not be transmitted farther. But if it were transmitted 1,000 or 2,000 feet, that would be quite enough to span an international stream and convey it from Canada to the United States. If the power is to be used in the form of hydraulic power for certain purposes, either the machinery must be connected direct with the waterwheel or the power must be transmitted by some means. If you transform it into electrical energy, you have to add two sets of machinery. You have to generate the electric current, and then you have to transmit it to the motor. Thus you greatly increase the cost of the power, and tlie Canadian consumer should not be placed at a disadvantage in that respect. I can illustrate that in this way. So far as I am aware, it is not practicable to operate pulpwood grinders by electrical energy, and nowhere is it done. Attempts have been made to do it, and there are perhaps favourable conditions at some places; but no engineer or business man acquainted with the operation of such works will for a moment deny that if it is done at all, it is done at 72
a disadvantage and at a very much enhanced cost. In certain cases it is utterly impracticable to use power for that purpose unless you can get direct connection with the waterwheel, either by connecting the grinders with the shaft of the waterwheel, or by belting or cable and that is one very important purpose for which power is used. In the case to which I refer, where some little difficulty arose, that was the trouble. It was at Fort Frances, where there is a power developed on an international stream. 15,000 horse-power from that development is to-day being used on the American side in a power-house built for the purpose of operating wood pulp grinding machines. There the grinders are connected direct with the shafting of the waterwheel, while on the Canadian side the difficulty arose because the company refused to permit any Canadian user to connect with the wheels, although there is a Canadian power-house in which power is developed, and although the plans that were filed, upon which the work was authorized, showed that the grinders were to be connected direct with the waterwheels on the Canadian side as well as on the American side. However, that is only an incident that might occur in any other place as well as there, and it seems to me the Act should provide for it. My reason for referring to these difficulties is that the department having the administration of this Act, chapter 16, interpreted it practically in the light in which I am proposing to amend it, because they asked the company to name the prices at which they would supply power to Canadian consumers by a series of questions. In those questions they asked the price for mechanical and hydraulic power as well as the price for electrical power; and indeed the regulations founded on the Act provide for fixing a price. There is really a necessity for the amendment if the Act is to be made more workable and plain, and if we are to remove difficulties which at present retard the use of power in Canada. I will take the liberty of reading some of the regulations founded on chapter 16, and dated November 7, 1907. Section 8 of those regulations reads as follow's :
Where a supply of electrical energy, gas or fluid is provided in any part of Canada by the contractor for export and home consumption, then the price charged to any person or company in Canada by the contractor shall not exceed the prices at which electrical energy, gas or fluid is sold by the contractor for export in like quantities under like circumstances.
In the regulations the generating company is referred to as the contractor. The protection here provided for Canadian users of power falls a good deal short of what appears to me should have been provided or perhaps urns the intention to provide. There is no safeguard



in that clause of the regulations against a great many contingencies, that can arise. All the company has to do is not to sell its power at all, but to use it itself. Then there would be no price at which the exported power was sold, and that provision of the regulations would not come into play. That is exactly what occurred at Fort Frances. The portion of power exported was not sold, but was used by the generating company, and no price has been fixed by them for power on the American side, for either the American or Canadian portion of the power, or for the power which they desire to take from Canada for use, after they have supplied the Canadian consumer. Therefore, I think provision should be made for the fixing of prices, and I propose the following in substitution for section 5 :
5. Any such license shall provide that the quantity of power or fluid to he exported shall be limited to the surplus, after the licensee has from time to time, as in this Act provided, supplied power or fluid and has also provided all proper means of applying such power or fluid for use by consumers in Canada, to the extent defined by such license.
Every such license shall stipulate:
(a)	The price at which power shall be supplied for municipal, domestic, commercial, manufacturing and other purposes for use in Canada.
(b)	The conditions and regulations under which the respective units of power shall be supplied.
(c)	The methods to be employed in supplying power, the methods of distribution and the hours of service.
I submit that it can be no hardship to any company or person dealing with power under these circumstances if he is asked, previous to getting a license, to fix the price at which he will furnish power _ to Canadian consumers and the conditions and methods of service under which the power will be delivered. It seems to me that should necessarily be provided for, and the amendment seeks to provide for it. Then, there is the following section:
3. Every such license shall provide power for use in Canada for any of the purposes aforesaid upon the request of any municipal corporation or of any bona fide applicant for power or energy, and such license shall supply such power within a reasonable time after such request.
That is practically what the Act now provides, but the word ' municipality ' is introduced. It seems to me that where a demand is made by a municipality upon a company for power or to fix the price,, the company cannot very well complain that to comply with that request is a hardship. The Act provides that prices may be regulated by the Governor in Council, and that is not interfered with by these amendments. Where that power exists, it Mr. CONMEE.
can operate no hardships to have it defined. I submit that in the case I am dealing with, we are carrying out practically the intention of legislation which has already passed this House. I refer to chapter 139, intituled an Act Respecting the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, and to the latter part of section 4 of that Act The section provides for the settlement of disputes and the fixing of prices, &c., by the Railway Board of Canada. And the latter lines of the section read as follows:
Such disputes shall, notwithstanding the provisions of section 13 of the Railway Act of 1903, be settled by the Railway Board of Canada on the application of any user or applicant for power or of the company or of the town of Fort Francis.
That same principle is embodied in these amendments. The other provisions in these amendments do not disturb the Act as it stands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I desire to make an explanation in regard io a matter which was before the House yesterday on a motion of my hon. friend i'rcm New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Tavlor), for certain papers. There seemed to be a question as to a fact which I had stated, and, as I had not the details before me at the time, I was not able to give the House the case as I understood it. If I may, I would like to do so now. The matter related to the issue of a patent to one Fanny Louise Irwin and to certain legal proceedings by the Justice Department to secure the cancellation of the patent on account of it having been issued in error, so that there might be substituted for it, a patent which would convey the title which was originally intends, to be conveyed. I find on reference to the papers, that the homestead was taken by one Thomas Vance, who squatted upon it in 1888. He made application for homestead entry on October 19, 1891. He applied for patent on July 22, 1892, and the issue of patent was approved by JJre Commissioner of Dominion Lands and certificate of recommendation issued by him November 11, 1892. This gave to Thomas Vance an assignable right under the regulations, which provides,

under section 28:
A person whose homestead may have been recommended for patent by the local agent or senior clerk, and who has received from such agent or clerk a certificate to that effect in the form K in the schedule to these regulations, countersigned by^ the Commissioner of Dominion Lands, or in his absence, by any member of the Dominion Lands Board, may legally dispose of and convey, assign or transfer his right and title therein.
On the 7th December, 1895, the agent at New Westminster forwarded an assignment from Thomas Vance to Fanny Louise Ir-wm, dated November 30, 1895, and on the 24th December, 1895, the department replied, stating that the assignment in question had been registered in the books of the department and that the land stood in M.iss Irwin's name. That is to say, Fanny Louise Irwin acquired, under the law, the right to a patent to this particular land without any notice of any reservation therein. That was the question of fact between myself and my hon. friend from New Westminster. The department was in fault

in afterwards granting the patent to Fanny Louise Irwin-but the patent was granted to her because she had already acquired tier rights from Thomas Vance and under the law-without notice of any reservation in the right that was given to Thomas Vance. So, Fanny Louise Irwin was in exactly the same position when she applied for her patent, as the assignees of Fanny Louise Irwin are now, in contesting the r:ght of the limit holders to the timber on that limit.
What was the date of the license to cut timber ?

speechtext: Before that motion is put, I desire to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister, if he has any knowledge of the whereabouts of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) at the present time. I would ask whether he is away, if he has permission to he away, and to engage in the work he is now doing in the county of Kings, Nova Scotia. My reason for asking this question is that about a week ago, when we were in supply, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), placed before us an item of $100,000 to build a barracks in the city of Montreal, and nobody in the House knew anything about these barracks, and consequently, we could not vote the supply. We had to drop it for the reason that the Minister of Militia was not in this House, and he has not been in this House from 'that, day to this. As I was anxious to know his whereabouts, I made inquiries, and I found in a paper published in Kentville, Nova Scotia, called the ' Western Chronicle,' of January 19, the following item of news:-

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Political meetings in the interest of the Liberal party, addressed by the . candidate, H. H. Wickware, K.C., Sir F. W. Borden, A. E. Wall, M.P.P., and other prominent citizens will be held as follows: Port Williams, January 21; Delhaven, January 23; Halls Harbour, January 24; Wolfville, January 25.
Now Mr. Speaker, the reason these meetings are being held is that a by-election is going on for the local legislature in the province of Nova Scotia. speechtext:
I used the round figures ' fifteen years ago it is fourteen years ago since the policy of the Hon. Mr. Fielding was adopted. At all events, I said that I used the words ' fifteen years ago.' Now my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) says that I drew the attention of the House to the fact that some of the newspapers had used the words ' twenty-five,' some others ' twenty ' and some others ' fifteen.' I think I have corroboration from him, because he has read from the evening papers, ' La Patrie ' and ' La Presse,' words to that effect. But, there is a better means of settling this great difficulty. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) and my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) were present at the dinner. Now, to settle this very serious question, I am ready to throw myself into the arms of the leader of the opposition. If I really used the words ' twenty-five years ago,'
I am very guilty indeed for having deceived this House, but I am quite positive, and I am quite sure my hon. friend from Pictou is quite positive, too, that I used the words ' fifteen years ago.' There is another point. My hon. friend seems to take exception to the compliments I paid before this very representative gathering to the memory of Sir John Macdonald and Sir George Etienne Cartier. The Manufacturers' Association of Montreal is an organization composed of the most important members of the Conservative party and one in which the Liberals are to a large extent in the minority, although I have always been on very friendly terms with both parties in that organization. But, my hon. friend seems to be under this delusion that a member of a Liberal government, speaking in the city of Montreal before manufacturers belonging to the Conservative party, is simply playing with them by saying something before them which he would not have the cour-

age to repeat in the House of Commons of Canada. Let me tell my hon. friend that the compliments, and deserved compliments, I as a young Canadian paid to the giants of the Conservative party of 30 and 40 years ago, I am ready to repeat before the House of Commons. I hope that if ever my hon. friend is invited to speak before the Manufacturers' Association, and that if it comes to his mind he should say something in praise of Alexander Mackenzie, the great Reform Prime Minister of Canada, he will not be afraid to pay the memory of that great man a little compliment, as I did to the memory of Sir John Macdonald.

speechtext:
It may not be a matter of great moment, but now that the subject has arisen, I may say that I was present at that dinner, and I heard a gentleman whom I believe to be the Postmaster General deliver an address, and I can say positively that the word * fifteen ' was not used, but that the words ' twenty years ' were used, as stated by the leader of the opposition. On that occasion the gentleman who sat beside me remarked that instead of using the word twenty, the Postmaster General should have mentioned thirty-two years. However, as is the custom with the Postmaster General, he was very pleasing and gracious on that occasion, and I thought it a particularly happy thing that he, as spokesman of the government of this country, should pay a well merited tribute to the fact that there was still in
effect the policy inaugurated by Sir John A. Macdonald, to whom the Postmaster General made reference. I thought it a splendid tribute by the Postmaster General that he should state that fact at a gathering of that kind, because our Liberal friends are disposed to admit, outside of this House, but not inside of this House, that we are to-day living, in effect, under the National Policy as laid down by Sir John Macdonald. I am sorry that, in spite of the admiration I hold for'the Postmaster General, he should see fit to be influenced by the sentiments of a few free trade protectionists, who support the government, and should find it necessary to revamp his remarks. I can understand that in addressing an audience one does not speak with the same accuracy as he would write, but 1 have a positive recollection of the incident at that, dinner, and so far as my ears can be relied upon, the facts are as I have stated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
subtopic: THE POSTMASTER GENERAL AND THE FISCAL POLICY OF CANADA.
speechtext:
The fact that my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) thought this incident of sufficient importance to bring it before the House a second time, is an evidence of the lack of material in the possession of hon. gentlemen opposite to attract the attention of the people of this country. I attended the dinner referred to, and I may say it was a delightful dinner, where all seemed to enjoy themselves, and I was seated in the immediate proximity of the Postmaster General.
I do not know what is responsible for the lack of memory and accuracy evidenced by some hon. gentlemen opposite, but certainly those who sat at the guests' table, in my immediate proximity, are aware of the fact that the Postmaster General used the words ' fifteen years.' The mental calculation was made at the moment that was made by my hon. friend from Assiniboia a moment ago who was so technical that he wanted to draw the inference that because the Postmaster General used the words fifteen years he was referring to some imaginary policy the Conservatives had in the year they went out of power. But there were other gentlemen present who did make the calculation, and they saw that, as we were now in 1911, and as the Liberal party came into power in 1896, the Postmaster General was sufficiently accurate in describing the period from which Canada's prosperity began to date. That was the period to which the Postmaster General referred, and that was the date from which Canada's prosperity began.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I wish to direct the attention of the government and the House to a resolution, notice of which was given before the adjournment of the House last evening. It reads as follows :

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted therefor: ' In the opinion of this House the action of the government in renting certain buildings in the city of Ottawa at prices which give the owners annually from 15 to 18 per cent net on the cost of their property is unbusinesslike, indefensible, and merits the censure of this House.
In 1909 my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works leased on behalf of the government a building on the corner of O'Connor and Queen streets, in the city of Ottawa, known as the Regal Building, for five years, with the privilege of renewing the lease for another term of five years, at an annual rental ot $16,095.73. The owners of the property are required by the lease to pay the city taxes, which amount annually to $1,186.07, for tw* stone walks that were put down by the city corporation $24.13 per annum, and for two roadways $75.75 per annum; and they will, of course, pay the insurance upon 'the building, which if insured for $50,000 at the rate of 65 cents per annum per $100, makes an annual payment of $325.	These sums make
a total of $1,610.95 which has to be paid by the owners of the building. Deducting tins amount from the annual rental paid by the government leaves the net amount paid by the government to the owners of this property at $14,484.80 per annum. Now, the first question that arises is why should the government rent this building at all? This property was owned originally by the Young Men's Christian Association of this city. They were seeking a purchaser for it for upwards of a year and a half. The right hon. the Prime Minister had taken into his government a brand new administrator in the person of the hon. Minister of Labour, and the government were seeking new quarters for my hon. friend. So, I presume the Minister of Public Works was approached by the Minister of Labour, and although the Minister of Public Works was well aware that this property was for sale and could be purchased by the government if they had any faith at all in the policy of government ownership. But my hon. friend decided that it was much better to rent the property from his supporters ; and so the middleman, who has been so much talked about in this House, and in this country, appears on the scene, and purchases the property from the Young Men's Christian Association in 1909 for the sum of $47,500. The owners of the property expended upon it a little less than $32,500, adding two new stories; so that their total investment was $80,000. On this amount the net rental they receive from the government gives them the handsome return of 18 per cent per annum after they have paid all their charges. I cannot understand why

the hon. Minister of Public Works did not arrive at the conclusion that it would be in the interest of the people of this coun-trv. if not in the interest of the government, that he should take some of the boasted surpluses that we have heard so much about for the last 15 years, and purchase this property, which it was well known to everybody, was on the market. But my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works is well versed in the methods of dealing with property in the interest of his friends in the city of Ottawa as well as in other parts of Canada, and he concluded that the policy of public ownership of tins building would not suit the government. So the middleman steps in and purchases the property. There are some other charges on the property which have to be paid by the government, such as water rates, lighting and heating, the caretaker's salary, and the operating of the elevator. The basement and the first and second floors are occupied, or are supposed to be occupied, by the Minister of Labour and his staff, the third floor by the Minister of Militia, and the top story by the Finance Department. I had the pleasure of going through the building the other afternoon, and I found in the top story one room about 30 feet square in which there was nothing at all. And alongside of it another room, not quite the same size, and in that story at present, notwithstanding the fact that my hon. friend has rented it at this enormous price, and has had it rented for more than 12 months, there are five vacant rooms absolutely unoccupied. The Militia Department, a little lower, is not at all crowded because there are several vacant rooms in that part of the building. The Minister of Labour is brand new of course, and he has filled up his department metty well except the basement, about one-quarter of which is not occupied. Therefore I am quite safe in saying that a little more than one-third of this building, for which we are paying this enormous rent, is not occupied at all. I do not wish to criticise too closely my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, but every man who has resided in Ottawa for the last few years realizes that property in this city has been rapidly increasing in value, and my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), when he came into power was well acquainted with the city and its outlook. One of the things for which the people of this country, and the opposition in particular, condemn my right hon. friend and his government, is that, notwithstanding the opportunities given them to purchase property at low prices they have allowed these opportunities to go by and rented from their friends at enormous prices. I may say that if my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works had taken out of the
treasury $80,000, the amount put into these premises by the owners or had borrowed it at 4 per cent-if he had taken out of the treasury $80,000 to purchase and improve this property and allowed 6 per cent on the investment, it would have been a fair investment, considering the increase in value from year to year, and if he had taken the balance of the amount paid these gentlemen-being the difference between 6 per cent and 18 per cent-in eight and a half years the government would have owned the building altogether and have had in addition $2,320.80 in the treasury. Why did not my hon. friend adopt that policy? It is not only yesterday that these gentlemen have been seeking for properties in the city of Ottawa. They have been on many streets in the city finding properties that were once owned by Conservatives find now owned by Reformers, looking up properties, in the interest, not of the people, but of their friends in the capital. The condemnation I have to offer is that my hon. friend lias been more careful of the interests of his political friends than of the great trust vested in him as Minister of Public Works. I am not going to add one statement after another in respect to public buildings, but I present this as a clear cut statement of the unbusinesslike policy of the Minister of Public Works.

Yes, a privilege to the government that makes it all the worse in my opinion. The assessed value of this property by the city when it was owned by the Y.M.C.A. was $30,000. If he has any criticism to make about the amount expended by the present owners $32,500, I answer by saying that after it was improved and enlarged, the assessment was increased from $30,000 to $55,000 by the city. Therefore there cannot be much doubt as to the amount expended upon it. The opposition and the newspapers have been criticising this government for allowing middlemen to step in between the people and the administration; the Liberal Conservative party moved a resolution condemning tl'.is government for allowing these middlemen to enter in and supply goods without public competition. In the Marine Department, in the Department of Railways and Canals, properties and goods were purchased from middlemen who repealed enormous profits in connection with the Intercolonial railway, and in connection with their busi-

ness. In the Department of Militia, articles were purchased at enormous prices from middlemen, and when difficulties arose in some of the departments, American bookkeepers were brought in and paid to straighten out the books of the department at $15 each per day. According to the Auditor's statement of the Printing Bureau scandals, the country lost more than $70,000 by purchasing goods outside the country, and giving the advantage to foreigners. These conditions the people are anxious should be done away with. The policy of the Liberal Conservative party is that no middleman shall live at the expense of Canada; that middlemen shall not be allowed to stand between the people and the government and make enormous profits, in one instance of 185 per cent.

The people will expect my hon. friend to explain how it is the government leased these premises from their own supporters, when they might have purchased in the open market, and when by so doing they would have saved the country these thousands of dollars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow Mr. Speaker to read the two resolutions, his and mine?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker has just sent it to me, and the word ' net ' is in the resolution. maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that I did say net profit, and I repeat that it is in both resolutions. And I am not at all excited, as my hon. friend seems to be just now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: ' Hansard ' will show whether my hon. friend used the word ' net ' or not. maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want an answer?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: My answer is that two lion, gentlemen will follow in this discussion, and they will give other buildings, and we will increase them to half-a-dozen if necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has said that, and I can only regret that he did not himself go into details as to all the buildings on which he invited his hon. friends to make their remarks to the House, before I was called upon to reply on behalf of the government. I appeal to you, Sir, and I appeal to members on both sides of this House, if that would not have been a fair course to pursue. What does my hon. friend do? He makes a charge against the government. He is the gentleman who makes the substantive motion, he simply makes a charge in regard to one building, and I, assuming that is the only charge that is to be made to-day, rise for the purpose of replying. Then the hon. gentleman proposes, after I have made my answer as head of the Department of Public Works, to call upon other gentlemen to make their charges, to which I will have no opportunity of making reply during this discussion. Whatever my hon. friend may think of that course, I am quite sure it is not one which will commend itself generally to* the good judgment of members of this' House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think I am responsible for that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
Clearly my hon. friend must be, because his statement evidently shows that he is in concert with other hon. gentlemen who are to follow up his charges and refer to other buildings, different from the one to which he has referred. Now let me say that with regard to the charge the hon. gentleman makes that I should have invited my colleagues to approve a considerable time ago of the purchase of the Regal building from the Young Mens' Christian Association, I am quite willing that the charge of the hon. gentleman, so far as that is concerned, shall be judged by the House and by the country. I did not think it was desirable for the government to be going around the city of Ottawa purchasing buildings for the temporary accommodation of the different departments, becoming owners of them, and I am satisfied that had I done so the hon. gentleman, instead of commending me for purchasing those properties, would have been the first to condemn me and to say that I should have made some temporary arrangement for the rental of buildings. It is to be remembered that we have already taken large appropriations for the purchase of land and for the construction of the new departmental block which is to be erected upon Mackenzie avenue and Sussex street. Does my hon. friend think that in view of Mr. BLAIN.
that fact, when we propose a very large expenditure which will run into three or four million dollars, including land, in view of the fact that we are making provision for housing all the different departments of the government, does he think that I would have been justified in making the purchase of the Regal building for the government? Yet the hon. gentleman says that it would have been much better to do that instead of renting the building. When the new departmental block is finished, we expect we will no longer need the Regal building, or a good many other buildings which are rented in different parts of the city. So much with regard to the charge that I ought to have purchased the property.
With reference to the rental, my hon. friend says that this building only cost the present owner the sum of $47,500. I do not know whether my hon. friend is correct as to that, I have no knowledge of what the building cost. Then my hon. friend states that the owners have expended upon it the sum of $32,500. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not understand that the cost of this building has been under investigation before the Public Accounts Committee; I do not understand that there has been any evidence given before any committee of this House as to what the owners have expended on that building. I would be glad if my hon. friend would give me the source of his information as to the expenditure by the owners.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: I will be very glad to do so, I will be glad to take this matter up in the Public Accounts Committee with the hon. gentleman, and I will be able to substantiate every statement I have made this afternoon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: And yet Mr. Speaker, today, in answer to a courteous invitation to my hon. friend

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend accept the challenge?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: In answer to a courteous request that my hon. friend should give me the source of his information as to the expenditure, the hon. gentleman declines to do so. And yet, Mr. Speaker, without affording to this House the source of his information as to the expenditure by the owners, not giving to this House a particle of information which they should require as to what the owners have expended upon the building-because my hon. friend could not have personal knowledge of that himself-he asks this House to condemn the Department of Public Works because they have paid the rental to which lie has referred.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say the figures are incorrect?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: I know nothing about them, one way or the other, I do not profess to know anything about the figures. But I would be very sorry indeed to ask this House to condemn the department in tills matter unless I was prepared to furnish the House with positive proof of the . amount which was expended, and to give to the minister and the House the source of my information, if I were in the place of my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: I am prepared to do that in the manner I have suggested.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
It seems to me that the hon. gentleman, having made the statement, owes it to this House, and owes it to himself, to give the source of his information, so that the House may judge as to whether that information can be relied upon. Now, Sir, with regard to the owners of the property, the hon. gentleman has made the charge that we dealt with a middleman. Let me say to my hon. friend that I throw back at him that charge, and I say there is not a shadow of foundation for it. The department has not dealt with a middleman, the department has dealt with the owner of the property, and with him alone. There has been no middleman concerned with, or dealt with, or negotiated with. When the first negotiations began, when I first heard of the subject of renting this property, it was owned by Dr. Hanna of this city," whether any other gentlemen were associated with him, I do not know. The hon. gentleman speaks of political friends of the government. -Sir, I do not know what the politics of Dr. Hanna are, I do not know whether he is a Liberal or Conservative. But I say that we dealt with him as a business man, and simply as a business man. The accommodation which could be provided in this building was convenient for the department, and we had an opportunity to rent the building from Dr. Hanna. We made every inquiry, we had examined it thoroughly, it was reported on by the officials of my department, and we agreed upon the rental. If my hon. friend had taken the trouble to inquire as to what rental is being paid for buildings similarly situated and of similar value in other parts of the city, he would have found that the rental is a very reasonable one indeed. Now, Sir, when we rent buildings for my department we do not enter upon the business without due consideration, and do not agree upon the rental or the terms without exercising the utmost care.
I do not personally intervene until all the information has been acquired, and until the reports of the proper officers in the department are made. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, the rental which is being paid per square foot for this building. and that is the only way in which you can judge as to whether the rental is
a reasonable one or not. We pay 81 -28 cents per square foot of space. We have made inquiries as to what rental is being paid in other buildings, and I find that upon Sparks street, in the ' Citizen ' building, a building which would be no better adapted for departmental offices than this, the average rental is 90 cents per superficial foot, and that includes all parts of the building which are rented as against 81 -21 cents per -square foot for this building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: What street is that on?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: The ' Citizen ' building is upon Sparks street.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: There is a difference in the value of property on that street, and the street on which that other building is situated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Not very much of a difference. As far as the ground floor is concerned I suppose there would foe quite a difference, but the Regal building is admirably situated for a departmental building, and we pay 81 -28 cents in rental as compared with 90 cents which the owners of the ' Citizen ' building receive. Then we also made inquiry regarding the Carleton chambers upon Sparks street, and we have been informed that the owner of that building receives $1.25 per superficial foot of space or 44 cents per superficial foot more than we pay for the Regal building. Then, Mr. Speaker, there is a building which was rented quite a number of years ago when property was not so valuable as it is today in the city of Ottawa because we all agree with what the hon. gentleman stated that real estate is advancing with great rapidity in Ottawa. Does my hon. friend not know that one of the absolute essential and certain results of the advancement of real estate is that rents go up because it is the rental which a person receives which largely determines the value and, as real estate goes up, of course, the owners charge a larger rental. The Corry building was rented some years ago for the purpose of the Railway Commission, and the amount that is paid for that including taxes is 9G 50 cents per superficial foot, or 15 cents per superficial foot more than we pay for the Regal building. If I am any judge I would say that the Regal building is just as well situated as the Corry building is. When the Corry building was rented inquiries were made as to what accommodation could be got in other parts of the city, and what other buildings were available, and after very careful consideration, as I am informed, the Corry building was rented, and the rental for that including the taxes is 15 cents per square foot more than we are paying for the Regal building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister, if, in renting these buildings, he does not take into consideration the location of the property that is on the most valuable streets. He is giving us the rentals on the main street in the city of Ottawa as compared with those on a back street.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Necessarily the 'experts of the department would do that, hut still we also have to consider the description, and the conveniences of the building because all these enter iiito the consideration. On Sparks street there might be a building which would not be at all adapted, or well adapted, for housing the officials of a department. My hon. friend knows that in each department-or, speaking generally, it is the case-there is a large number of clerks to be accommodated as nearly as possible in the one building ; at all events, the clerks who are engaged in a particular branch of a department must necessarily be housed in one building. It is not every building that will accommodate them, and there are very few buildings on Sparks street which will be suitable for the accommodation of the officials of a department. For the Railway Commission building we pay 98-48 cents per superficial square foot or 17 cents per square foot more than we pay for the Regal building. Then, Mr. Speaker, take the Canadian and the Woods buildings. I suppose I shall have to refer to these because I presume that my hon. friend, with that wisdom of which he appears to be so proud, has kept back the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) in order to bring up the Woods building and the Canadian building after I have taken my seat ; therefore, it will be necessary for me to make reference to the Canadian building, and the Woods building. I have heard it said that the Imperial Realty Company receive an exorbitant rent for those buildings, I have gone into the matter very carefully, and I am prepared to assert in this House what is my belief that the Imperial Realty Company only receive a net revenue of a shade over 7 per cent on their investment in those buildings. I am speaking now of the Canadian building, the Woods building, and the Queen street building, and I say that they are receiving a revenue of a shade over 7 per cent. I remember, Sir, that before the Committee on Public Accounts, there was an attempt made to show that the Woods and Canadian buildings had only cost somewhere between $200,000 and $300,000. The hon. member for North Ontario called somebody who had had a contract simply for the four walls, and floors of the building, or rather he tried to impress the committee with the fact that the evidence of this witness

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
showed that it had cost $100,000, and this sum practically represented the whole cost of the building. He called Mr. Charles Holbrook of the firm of Holbrook & Sutherland, the gentleman who had built the four walls and floors of these two buildings-the Woods building, and the Canadian building, and I find on page 452 of the evidence taken before the Public Accounts Committee that Mr. Holbrook makes this statement :
Q. I would like to ask you as a practical man, what would you say would be the value of the Woods building at the present time?- A. I take it about $300,000-from $250,000 to $275,000.
That, Mr. Speaker, is entirely outside of the land which has to be added as a part of the cost. In regard to the other building, Mr. Holbrook says that it is larger, and that it will be worth about $300,000. If Mr. Holbrook is right in putting the value of the Woods building at $275,000, the value of the Canadian building would be very considerably more because it contains at least 200,000 cubic feet more than the Woods building. Assuming that Mr. Holbrook's value of the Woods building is correct, I would think that it would bring the value of the Canadian building up to from $350?000 to $375,000, or $380,000 at the very least to which also would have to be added the value of the land.
The Queen street building, with the land, would be something like $65,000 or $70,000, and if your add these two together and then take the ordinary expenses of insurance, and wear and tear, and cost of management, I believe the net revenue would only be a shade over seven per cent. The hon. gentleman from North Ontario, if he speaks on this question will possibly tell you that these properties are assessed at very much less than the valuation of Mr. Holbrook, but I think it will be generally agreed that the assessment value is not always a correct test of the value of a building. The hon. gentleman from Peel told us that the Regal building, although it cost about $50,000, and although the present owners have spent about $30,000 on it making $80,000, it is only assessed at $50,000, which would show that the assessors do not attempt to get near the value of these large buildings. Then, we have had it in evidence before the Public Accounts Committee that the cubic contents of the Canadian building are something over 1,200,000 feet, while the cubic contents of the the Woods' building are between 900,000 and 1,000,000 cubic feet. We have also had it in evidence by Mr. Ewart, the chief architect, that speaking roughly the fair average cost of a fire-proof building would be 30 cents per cubic foot, and taking the cubic contents of the Canadian building at 1,200,000 feet you would get $360,000 as the fair value of that build-

ing. To that, you have to add the value of the land. The hon. gentleman from North Ontario said this land was only assessed at a few thousand dollars, but that was a number of year ago, and to-day no expert in real estate would say that the land occupied by the Canadian building is not to-day easily worth between $40,000 and $50,000, that the land on which the Woods5 building stands is not easily worth between $30,000 and $40,000, and the land of the Queen street building is not easily worth upwards of $20,000. Now, the total rental paid for the Canadian building and the Woods' building and the Queen street building is $72,000 per annum. If you take the valuation of these buildings with the land as being in the vicinity of $800,000 which I believe is a fair valuation for these three properties, you will find that after paying expenses of management and wear and tear and other charges that rental would give a little over 7 per cent, which, the evidence before the Public Accounts Committee shows is what the Imperial Realty Company gets out of these buildings. There is another very good way of testing whether or not we are paying too high a rental for these buildings. If you take the total amount we pay, including one-half the cost of the building of partitions, &c., which was paid by the government, it would amount in the case of the Canadian building to 96 09 cents per square foot. But if you distribute the cost of these improvements over the ten years during which the government has arranged to occupy that property you will find that it figures out at 60 -85 cents per square foot, and it is one of the very cheapest properties which the government has been able to rent in the city of Ottawa. Of the three buildings which the government rents from the Imperial Realty Company, it is a remarkable fact that for the Queen street building, as to which there has been no criticism by hon. gentlemen opposite, we are actually paying 98 48 cents per square foot, or more than we are paying for the other buildings. Hon. gentlemen opposite have for a long time been criticising the rent we are paying for the Canadian building and the Woods' building, but they have never had one word of criticism in regard to the building on Queen street occupied by the Railway Commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: We are coming to that building later.	[DOT]

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

My hon. friend has been a long time getting to it. Now, as to the value of these buildings. It was proved before the Public Accounts Committee that in the year 1908-I am not sure whether that was before the government rented the second portion of the Canadian building,
but it was about that time-it was proved before the committee that the, Imperial Realty Company which owns this building had, according to the evidence of Mr Finnie, manager of the Bank of Ottawa, purchased it from Mr. J. W. Woods for $1,000,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: That was in stock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
It was stock, but it must be borne in mind that while Mr. Woods received stock for the building, there were, as Mr. Finnie swore, a number of other gentlemen who bought stock in the company, and who would therefore be interested greatly in the value of the property because they were investing their money in it. However, in 1908, the company was proposing to raise money upon the security of these buildings, either through or from the Royal Trust Company. The property consisted of the Canadian building, the Woods' building, the Queen street building, and two other small properties of comparatively little value. As an act of precaution, the Royal Trust Company caused a valuation of this property to be made, and I shall read the report as to that valuation. The valuation was made by two experienced men, Mr. A. Pratt, formerly city assessor, and Mr. James Mather, a prominf ent and reliable architect in the city of Ottawa, and these gentlemen were engaged, not by Mr. Woods, or the Imperial Realty Company, but by this large financial institution in order to determine whether in justice to their shareholders they would be warranted in making an advance of $400,000 upon bonds to be issued against the property. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, it is very seldom that these companies lend over 50 per cent of the value of real estate. The Royal Trust Company was of course most desirous to have a correct valuation of this property.
Now, Sir, who are the Royal Trust Company? I suppose that if hon. gentlemen opposite did not know who they were they would be attempting to cast doubt upon their sincerity, and to insinuate that they had colluded with the Imperial Realty Company to boost the value of this property. The Royal Trust Company is a company closely allied with the Bank of Montreal. Its directors are: Right Hon. I.ord Strathcona and Mount Royal, president; Sir Edward Clouston, vice-president; Sir H. Montagu Allan, R. B. Angus, A. Baumgarten, E. B. Greenshields, C. M. Hays, C. R. Hosmer, Sir W. C. Macdonald, Hon. R. Mackay, A. Macnider, H. V. Meredith, David Morrice, James Ross, Sir T. G, Shaughnessy, Sir William C. Van Home. These are the directors of the Royal Trust Company, and when the Imperial Realty Company went to them in 1908 for a loan of $400,000 on first mortgage bonds, it was

expected that they would either lend the money themselves, or would, as a trust company, give the sanction of their name, which would enable the Imperial Realty Company to borrow this large sum on the property. I am told that the Royal Trust Company themselves underwrote the bonds. Therefore, you will see what value is to be attached to the report of their valuator, and I will take the liberty of reading that report. It is dated Ottawa, December 17, 1908. It is addressed to J. J. Gormully, Esq., barrister, &c., who, I presume, would be the solicitor of the Royal Trust Company, and is as follows:-

the expenses of management, the insurance end the local improvement tax; yet my hon. friend has taken no account of these, although, according to my information, the same information was given 'before the Committee on Public Accounts. speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to say that I made no statement as to the taxes, &c., in respect to the Royal buildingp I mentioned them all, and he will see them in * Hansard.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: I am now speaking of my hon. friend's resolution. I am not speaking of the emasculated speech with which he attempted to cut down the force of his resolution, and in which he simply referred to one building when he made a charge with respect to others. I am referring to his resolution, in which he says that we have rented buildings at 'prices which give to the owners from 15 to 18 per cent net on the cost of the properties.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: May I be permitted to ask whether that statement is correct with respect to the Regal building, to which I referred?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext: Is there any evidence on record that the Royal Trust Company put a dollar of their own money into that building? They lent the mojiey on the security of the rentals, but not their own money-other people's money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says the Royal Trust Company lent other people's money. As I understand, that is what a trust company does every day; it lends the money of other people. But it is trust money; it is the money of the widow and the orphan, which they are

bound to guard more securely and carefully than they would the money of their own shareholders; and there is the implied guarantee that they would exercise the utmost prudence in dealing with it. When I show now, following up the evidence of Mr. Holbrook before the Committee on Public Accounts by the valuation given by these experts of that land and building, according to which it was worth $288,350, that the rental we pay is only $25,777, apart from the heating, running the elevator and the taxes-this is what would come to the owners, out of which they have to pay insurance, cost of maintenance, wear and tear of the building and local improvement taxes. When I show all that and show that necessarily it would reduce the amount down to somewhere between 7 per cent and 8 per cent, surely the hon. gentleman would not ask this House to vote for a resolution, false on its face, declaring that we have been in the habit of renting buildings at prices which net to the owners a revenue of from 15 per cent to 18 per cent.
Parcel No. 3 being composed of lot 63 and broken lot 64 on the south side of Slater street and also being composed of the northerly portion of lot 63 and 64 on the north side of Laurier avenue (formerly Maria street); size about 121 feet in front and 226 feet in depth, superficial area 27,530 square feet. No. 4, Nos. 87 and 89 Laurier avenue, $13,300.
No. 5, lots 62 and EJ, 61 Laurier Avpuue, $23,565.

mentioned, of $36,000-$790,000 in round figures. Yet all that we pay for the Woods building, the Canadian building, and the Queen street building, is $72,000 per year, or a gross revenue to the owners of less than 10 per cent upon their value.
Mr. BLAlN. That does not include the Regal building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ABSENCE OF MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
speechtext:
No, I am speaking now of the' Woods building, the Canadian building, and the Queen street building. The Imperial Realty Company has nothing to do with the Regal building. The Royal Trust Company have nothing to do with it, as my hon. friend must know. I am reading the reports of the Royal Trust Company, which had the properties owned by the Imperial Realty Company examined, on which the latter were asking them to advance on their bonds the sum of $400,000, and this the Royal Trust Company did. The report concludes:
We the undersigned have carefully examined the several properties named in the above report and are of the opinion that the value set opposite each property is a fair cash value thereof, and that the total value of the five parcels of land is $828,060.
Out of that has to be taken the $13,300, and the $23,565, which are not rented to the government, leaving a net valuation of very close to $790,000. The rental upon the three buildings is $72,000, which would be less than 10 per cent on their valuation by these experts, and out of that the owners would have to pay the various charges for insurance, local improvement taxes, cost of management and wear and tear. The net result would be to give the Imperial Realtv Company a net dividend of a shade over 7 per cent on the moneys invested.
