Mr. Speaker, I had referred, before the recess, to a number of buildings which had been leased by the department, but there are a few others to which I have not yet referred. One is the Imperial building on Queen street, belonging to the estate of one Mr. Pearson. The net office area is 12,082 feet, and the rental has been $4,200 per annum, which would be at the rate of 35 -76 cents per superficial foot. This includes the power for the elevator, but the rest of the charges are borne by the government. We have agreed, upon the renewal of the lease, to make some increase in the rent, because it was lower than the building was fairly worth. Just what it will be I am not in a position to say at the moment. Then, there is another building occupied by the surveyor general's branch of the Department of the Interior, at the corner of Slater and Metcalfe streets. The net office area is 9,811 feet, and the rental $3,000 per annum. That is at the rate of 30-6 cents per superficial foot. We pay the taxes, heating and some other charges, which bring the total up to 45-26 cents per square foot. I gave the Trafalgar building, the rental of which is 79-81 per square foot; the Seybold building, the Corry building, the Canadian building, the Militia, or Woods, building, and the Railway Commission building.
Then, there is another building, a portion of which we are renting from the Molsons Bank, on Metcalfe street. It has an office area of 4,294 feet, and the rental we pay is $2,340, or at the rate of 54 -5 cents per superficial foot. We also rent some premises in the Great Northwestern Telegraph Company's building, 1,006 superficial feet, for which we pay $420 rental, which is 41 -75 cents per superficial foot. There is another building in which we rent premises; it is in the new station of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We have rented three flats there for the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission was very much Mr. PUGSLEY.
crowded for room in the building on Queen street, and we have had a very strong requisition from the members of the board that we should provide increased accommodation. We made an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company under which they will fit up three flats especially for the use of the Board of Railway Commissioners. At first they asxed us a rental of $23,000. We carried on negotiations for,
I think, about three months, and finally we succeeded in getting them to accept a rental of $19,500. That includes heating, elevator service and everything except lighting. My hon. friend may say that is higher than the rental we pay for some other buildings. So it is, but we get very superior accommodation, and, of course, we must have regard to the accommodation that is furnished. The building is to be specially fitted up for the accommodation of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I may say with reference to this, as with reference to the Woods, the Canadian and all the other buildings -which the government leases, that when the government ceases to occupy these buildings, as it will naturally do when the new departmental block is erected, the owners may have their buildings idle for a considerable time while they are making alterations to accommodate the buildings to the wants of the new tenants who may be desirous of renting.
Will the hon. gentleman give the floor area?

I was just about to give that. There are 23,758 superficial feet in the three flats, for which we are to pay, as I said, $19,500 per annum. That is at the rate of about 82 cents per superficial foot, -which includes heating and elevator service.	-
What I have done has been to refer all these matters with regard to rental, since I have been minister, to the proper officials of my department, and I feel sure, from the reports that they have made to me from time to time, and before recommending a rental to be agreed upon by me as head of the department, that they have made careful inquiry as to what rentals are charged by other owners of property in the city of Ottawa, and that they have based their recommendations accordingly. Let me call attention to the matter in another way for the purpose of showing that none of these rentals are excessive. When negotiating with "the Grand Trunk Railway Company we made inquiries as to what would be charged for property in thq city of Ottawa and as to \vhat would be charged for property in the city of Montreal. I found that for a building conveniently situated in the city of Ottawa the rental would run from 90 cents per superficial foot up to, I think, as high as $1.25 per superficial foot, while in the city of Montreal there are very few
JANUARY 24, i*n
offices and fiats in office buildings which are rented at a less rate than $1.50 per superficial foot. If lion, gentlemen desire to ascertain what would be a fair rental for an office in the city of Montreal they could make inquiry with regard to the point. They could go to the Messrs. Rosenthal, to the Canada Life Company, to Mr. Hope, who owns a new building which has recently been put up, to the ' Citizen ' Company, and to the owners of other buildings, which are conveniently situated in Ottawa, and I will venture to say that they will not be able to find that it would be possible to rent premises as conveniently situated as those which the government has rented at a less rental than the government is paying for the accommodation which it is now enjoying in these different buildings. And, Mf- Speaker, is not that the test?
Suppose my hon. friend's information is correct as to the price paid for the building formerly belonging to the Young Men's Christian Association by the present owners. As to that I know nothing, and the hon. gentleman has given us no evidence except his statement, which must be based upon hearsay. Is that the ground upon which we should act if we desire accommodation in the city of Ottawa, and, looking around, we find that accommodation can be had in a certain building? Are we to ascertain what the property was bought for? Is it not our duty rather to judge what the accommodation is worth to the government compared with what similar accommodation can be got for in other buildings in the city of Ottawa. I think that is the true test. If these gentlemen purchased the building for $50,000, they got a remarkably good bargain. I venture to say that that building with the land represents a cost to the association of a very much larger sum. The cost of this building to the government, including the heating and the lighting and the elevator service, does not exceed 81 -28 cents per superficial foot. For an office 15 feet square, that would be a little over $180 a year. Why, Sir, in the city of St. John, wliere real estate is not worth within 50 per cent of what it is in the city of Ottawa, $150 a year is regarded as a reasonable rent for an office of that size, which is heated and lighted and has elevator service. I doubt very much if any office accommodation can be got in Ottawa for a less price. My hon. friend has not gone around in Ottawa and sought information as to what other owners have got from other rented properties; he has not ventured to produce a single owner to testify what such premises are fairly worth; and yet, without a tittle of evidence to support him, he asks this parliament to say that I and my predecessors have been guilty of some great wrong for which we ought to be condemned. I think I have shown that we have exercised good judgment and have acted with reasonable prudence, and are paying no more as rental for these properties than would be obliged to pay to the other owners of similar properties. When the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Samuel Sharpe) comes to speak, he will say that there was a witness before the Committee on Public Accounts, who was a city assessor, and who assessed the Woods' building at 13 cents per cubic foot. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that is the basis on which the assessors value buildings of that character, which are fireproof in construction, and which have all modern conveniences, elevator accommodation, properly wired for electric lighting and provided with the best heating apparatus, all I can say is that they are assessing such property at only one-half of its cost, and less than one-half of its value. As against the statement of that witness, who is not a builder, we have the evidence of the gentleman who erected the Woods' building that it was worth in the vicinity of $270,000, and that the Canadian building which had 200,000 feet more of cubic contents, would be worth in the vicinity of $300,000. In addition to that, we have the Dominion architect, who estimates the cost of buildings which are not fireproof at not less than 23 cents per cubic foot, and buildings which are fire-proof at not less than 30 cents. As further evidence that these are thoroughly well built buildings, which are fire-proof, let me call attention to the fact that the owners receive the very lowest insurance rate which is put on the most up-to-date fire-proof buildings in Ottawa, being only 45 cents per $100 for a period of three years. There are many business men in this House who know that the insurance companies very rarely insure for more than from 75 to 80 per cent of the value; and these two buildings, which the appraisers of the Royal Trust Company have valued in the vicinity of $790,000, are insured for the sum of $590,-
000.
Now, Sir, in view of what I have stated with regard to these buildings-the Woods [DOT] building, the Canadian building, and the Queen street building; in view of the statement of the builder that the Woods building was worth from $250,000 to $275,000, and that the Canadian building would be worth in the vicinity of $300,000; in view of the fact that the appraisers of the Royal Trust Company have put the values of these three properties at about $790,000; in view of the fact that Mr. Woods some years ago disposed of these properties to the Imperial Realty Company, for stock, it is true, to the extent of a million dollars, but a considerable portion of which was sold to bona fide investors at what was regarded as a fair value; in view of the fact that the Royal Trust Company, who are the eus-

todians of the money of widows and orphans, and whose duty it is to see that that money is safely invested, and who, in accordance with the practice of loan companies, do not advance more than 50 per cent of the value of real estate, acted on a valuation of $800,000 when it lent $400,000 on the bonds on these properties; in view of the fact that the net rental, according to the figures I have given, only slightly exceeds seven per cent; I think my hon. friend cannot censure the government on the ground that they rented buildings which net the owners from 15 to 18 per cent. As to the other buildings we have no evidence whatever, as to the cost, but I have given you the average rental per superficial foot, I have spoken of the care exercised in renting these buildings, and I have challenged the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) to produce the testimony of a single witness before the Public Accounts Committee, or elsewhere that these offices are not worth the amount the government is paying, or that equally convenient accommodation could be obtained for less money elsewhere. The hon. gentleman has suggested that in respect to the Regal building, middlemen were employed. I deny it and I say that we knew no one in this transaction except the owner. The government desired this building for the accommodation of one of its most important departments and we rented it at so much per superficial foot, as we thought was reasonable and fair. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) says we rented it from friends of the government. Let me tell him that I have no knowledge whatever of the politics of Dr. Hanna, who owns the building, but on inquiry I am informed that he has never been identified with the Liberal party in this city. So far as I know he may be a Conservative or a Liberal when he casts his vote at the poll.
Who are his associates?

I do not know. Does the hon. gentleman know who they are? If he does he is at perfect liberty to mention their names to the House, and I invite him to do so. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that it is too much of a habit of my hon. friend and some other hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side to hurl insinuations in regard to middlemen and insinuations as to graft in connection with public buildings and public works. To-night and at all times I defy that hon. gentleman to show that so far as my department is concerned I have ever, in connection with public buildings or in connection with any other matter, employed a middleman to negotiate for a property. Every such transaction has been carried on between the department and the owners of the property and in the light of day. We did not buy the Regal Mr. PTTGSLEY.
building because we knew that in a few years when we had the new departmental block erected we would not require it, but accommodation was needed temporarily and we obtained it at a reasonable rent. We dealt directly with the owner and every transaction in connection with it was open and above board, and having negotiated for a considerable time we got it at the lowest rental and upon the best' possible terms. I have not examined in detail all the evidence given before the Public Accounts Committee, but I have cited the evidence of an experienced builder who erected the walls and the floors, and the evidence of two men whose duty it was to place a reasonable value upon it for the Royal Trust Company. I have given, and I defy my hon. friend to contradict it, what are considered fair rentals in this city and in Montreal, where the rentals per superficial foot for these office buildings are double what we are paying in Ottawa. I feel that I can appeal with the utmost confidence to the members of this House to say that the hon. gentleman who moved the motion has not presented the slightest evidence upon which he can ask the House to vote for this amendment. In view of the facts which I have presented, I think it is an insult to the intelligence of the members of the House to ask them to sustain such an amendment.

If, Mr. Speaker, I have any objection to the wording of this resolution, it is that it is too moderate and temperate in tone. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) finds the net return to the owners on the basis of the rent paid by the government as 18 per cent, but I think the facts will} show that the rent which the government are paying comes nearer 25, and even 30 per cent in many cases. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Peel deals generally with certain buildings, but the minister failed to answer the specific case made out by my hon. friend (Mr. Blain), although he lashed himself into a frenzy and fury in connection with a charge yet unmade in regard to the Canadian building and the Woods building. There is an old adage that a guilty conscience needs no accuser, and when the Minister of Public Works indulged in frenzy and fury in defending the Woods and Canadian buildings no doubt his conscience told him that, to use his mild term, the government was paying more than a shade over 7 per cent. The whole defence set up by the Minister of Public Works was based upon a wrong hypothesis. He rested his case with regard to the Woods building and the Canadian building on the valuation made by two men on behalf of the Royal Trust Company, but it is sig-

nificant that these two valuators were not produced as witnesses before -the Public Accounts Committee to tell us on what their valuation was based. I have heard . the Minister of Public Works object to accepting secondary evidence but there never was a clearer case of secondary evidence than the evidence he produced tonight, when the men who pretended to value the Canadian building and the Woods building were not called jbefore the Public Accounts Committee but their written report was put in. I am safe in assuming that their valuation wras based, not upon the actual value of the land and the cost of construction, but on the exorbitant and outrageous rentals guaranteed this company for ten yeaTS by this government. Any one who has any knowledge of the conditions in this country knows that a fair net return to a landlord is not much more than 6 per cent on his investment; and in Ottawa, by reason of the speculative value of property, landlords do not, according to the evidence of the city assessor, get more than 31 per cent net. The Minister of Public Works himself in this House said that 6 per cent was a reasonable return on money invested in real estate; but when he rented a building constructed by this government to one of the officials of this government, and was asked -what rent he was going to ask, he replied that he would ask for the reasonable return of 4 per cent. Yet he has been paying 25
per cent, in the case of the Woods building, as the landlord's net return, and 30 per cent on the Canadian building.
The hon. minister says that the assessment is not a proper method of calculating the cost of the building. I admit that in most cases the assessment will not show the actual cost of construction. But in this instance the assessor, when put in the box, was asked how he arrived at the estimate he had made, he replied that he compared the property with the valuations of other properties in the surrounding district and on that based his assessment. This assessment, however, was objected to by Mr. Woods. Mr. Woods said:	You have assessed too high and I want you to lower the amount; here are my books. And he opened his books and showed the assessor the cost of construction. The books of the Imperial Realty Company showed the cost of construction, and based on that cost, the return to W'oods and his associates is 25 per cent on the Woods building and 30 per cent on the Canadian building. In respect of those buildings, the assessor said they had a lifetime of 150 years, yet strange to say we are paying a return on their cost which will amount to a refund of the whole capital in four years in the one case and three and a third years in the other. In the case of the Woods building, the assessment of $110,000 was taken, so the assessor swore, from the books of the company which constructed the building. The real estate cost $5,500 and the total cost of building and real estate was $115,500. Yet on this building we are paying a rental of $25,777.20. And in addition we have spent on permanent improvements the sum of $15,675.74. In other words, with respect to the Woods building we are paying a net return of 25 per cent to the landlord and in addition have improved his property to the extent of $15,675. The Canadian building is assessed at $134,000, and the real estate at $7,800 or a total of $141,800. And for a building that only cost $141,800, we are paying a rental of $42,326.90, and in addition we have paid the exorbitant sum of $45,645.69 on permanent improvements. In

The method of calculating rent is one peculiar to the present administration. In all my experience, I never before heard of a tenant renting a whole building by the superficial foot. So that there would be a net profit to the company of $1,802,125 in .30 years, and they would still own the building free of any claim. Among the shareholders of this company are:-J. W. Woods, 550 shares; D. R. Finnie, 800 shares, in trust; G. C. Edwards, 100 shares, in trust; Sir H. M. Pellatt, 250 shares; and Judge McTavish. There are a number of other shareholders, but I have not the list under my hand. Now, the total rentals are:-On the Woods building, $25,777.20; on the Canadian building, $42,626.90; a total of $68,314.10. The government can borrow money at 31 per cent per annum, and hence with the annual sum of $68,314.10, have borrowed $1,951,830 with which they could have erected these buildings at a cost of $300,000, and then would have had $1,651,830 in the treasury to the good. That is to say: The rent equals net income at 31 per cent on an investment of $1,951,830, while the company expended less than $300,000 in the construction of both buildings, towards which we contributed $61,666.43 in permanent improvements. Now, I submit, in conclusion, that the people of this country do not desire the various departments, under the control of ministers who are paid high salaries, conducted in this manner. Again we find that the hon. Minister of Public Works was in Winnipeg last July, and while there he made some speeches, in which he said that the only charges brought against the government "were in reference to the sawdust wharf and the electric light contract, and these were utterly untrue. The Manitoba 'Free Press,' quoting his speech, under date of J uly 13, 1910, said:-
Mr. Pugsley touched upon some criticism which he had received from the leader of the
opposition (referring to the sawdust wharf and the electric light contracts). The charges dealt with were two, which Mr. Pugsley proved to have been absurd and unfounded.
The Winnipeg 'Telegram' also of July 13, 1910, quotes the hon. minister as making that statement with reference to the electric light contract:-
There was nothing in the transaction that was not straightforward, and the opposition dare not challenge me on the floor of the House, though they make bold to use these insinuations against me in their speeches outside of the House.
When you reflect that one of the good old principles of the Liberal party was ' the ancient and undoubted right of the House of Commons to inquire into all matters of public expense,' you wonder why these hon. gentlemen go to the Public Accounts Committees and use every effort in their power to strangle investigation and to suppress the facts. When. Mr. Ernest Linton, the secretary of 'the Imperial Realty Company, was in the witness box, as there were significant features about these contracts which impressed me very seriously, I asked him if there was any official of the Public Works Department who was residing in the Roxborough apartments. At first he refused to answer, bdt finally the chairman ruled that he had to answer. Then he said that the only officials who were residing in the Roxborough apartment were the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) and the hon. Minister of Public Works.
And I suppose my hon. friend suggests that we get free rent, does he?

I simply state what was the evidence of the secretary of the Imperial Realty Company, and the House and the country can draw their own inference. I say that the contracts were so outrageously unfair to the interests of this country that the right hon. the First Minister should appoint a royal commission to investigate the whole transaction from beginning to end.

Mr. Speaker, I think the House would have more highly appreciated the course of the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat if he had made the many charges which he has made throughout his speech, at a time when it was within the power of the Minister of Public Works to reply to him. It may be the practice of this House to entertain charges of this kind made in the partial manner in which these charges have been made; it may be the policy of the opposition to call the minister to his feet to reply when only a portion of the charges are made; but I venture to say that no fair-

minded man can have listened to the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat without coming to the conclusion that it is not a fair way in which to make charges of this character. The matters to which these charges relate are such as to be more within the knowledge of the hon. minister than of any other member of this House. He has control of them, he knows of them; matters which are unfamiliar to other members of the House are quite within his knowledge; and I have no doubt that had he the opportunity now to reply to the hon. member, he would answer him as completely and as fairly as he did the hon. member who made the motion. The hon. gentleman has recited the various leases in a way which tends to confuse the House in regard to the subject. One would think, from the manner in which he referred to them, that they all related to the same premises. If a little attention is paid to them, however, it will be found that the earliest one related to the east half of the Woods building, and as to that, the proprietor bore all the expenses of the alterations. The next related to the west half, and contained a clause by which the proprietor was to make the alterations and the government was to pay one-half the cost. The third lease related to the portion that was not included in either of the previous leases. There are two leases relating to the Canadian building, one for the west half, and the other for the east half. Now, to my mind, the question under discussion as to the propriety of the rentals paid must depend wholly upon the value of the buildings rented. It must be remembered that at the time the first lease was made there was a vast increase in the business of this country, and it was absolutely essential that the government should obtain premises in which that business could be properly carried on.	No one who is
familiar with the conditions in Ottawa as far back as 1903 can doubt that it	was utterly impossible for	the
government to secure another building as suitable for their purpose as the Woods building. At that time that was the only building in this city that could be secured. Of course it is easy to go back to many years ago when real estate in Ottawa could be bought for a song, when building was much cheaper, and take the valuation then as basis for an estimate, but that is not a fair way in which to arrive at a reasonable rental on these properties leased by the government. In making a lease for ten years, the rental is not based wholly on the value of the year of making, but on the return which the building ought to bring during the period covered by the lease. It may well be that the government, in this lease made in 1903, will be considerably the gainer, before 'its termination, Mr. CONGDON.
by the fact that the rental was fixed at that time.
I know of no way in which the value of real estate can be fixed except by taking the testimony of men who are accustomed to estimate such values. It would not have been possible to have brought before the committee better evidence of values than that given by the valuators to the Royal Trust Company. It is absurd to say that in 1908 the Royal Trust Company was influenced, in the loan it made to the Im-oerial Realty Company, by the fact that there were still a few years to run on the leases made in 1903 and 1905. That certainly would be a very -small element in determining the value put upon the buildings as security for the loan. Turning, then, to the report of these valuators, we have the most explicit evidence as to what they considered to be the values of these different buildings. We have these values defined in various ways. We have the Queen street property estimated to be worth $68,975. On this the rental paid is $5,300, and I do not think that can be called an excessive rental. The next lot is the Woods property, which is estimated as worth $288,350. There is a lease of that building reserving a rental of $25,777. The next building is the Canadian, estimated by these valuators at $433,870, and the rental is $43,536. Taking these various properties as estimated in this valuation, they aggregate $791,195, and the total rental is $73,000, very considerably less than 10 per cent, and only about 10 per cent if, from the $791,000 you deduct the amount paid by the government on alterations.
My hon. friend criticised the various provisions in the leases and the various transactions with regard to alterations, and apparently confused the leases. No doubt in the first lease the cost of the alterations was paid wholly by the proprietor, but only half in the second lease. And in a second lease it is not unusual for tne proprietor to change the terms of the first. No doubt in 1903 every one -who knew anything about real estate in Ottawa expected a prompt and quick rise in prices and values. In 1905, when the second lease was made, such a rise had taken place, and from time to time since there has been such an increase that the rentals paid by the government are fair and just, if you take the whole period covered by these leases and strike the average.
My hon. friend talked of a rake-ofi as though there was such a thing in respect to the heating and lighting. The evidence shows clearly that the Imperial Realty Company meant to obtain a larger amount for these purposes than they were entitled to, but the moment the minister discovered that the vouchers were not in accord with the amounts charged, he suggested that

action should be taken to cancel the contract.
My hon. friend charges some of the members of the Public Accounts Committee which investigated this matter with having obstructed the investigation, and put every obstacle possible in the way of securing a full disclosure. Well, in my opinion, no one can read the report of the evidence taken before that committee without coming to the conclusion that the very fullest and freest investigation was allowed. The very statement my hon. friend makes that the committee unanimously recommended the cancellation of this lighting contract shows that the committee was ready to do what was fair and just. There may have been one or two rulings of the chairman in which the hon. gentleman did not agree, but that frequently happens. In any court of justice one occasionally meets with decisions ruling out evidence, which decisions the counsel on one side is sure not to approve. But you cannot read the evidence given before the Public Accounts Committee without seeing that every possible opportunity was given to investigate these matters in every line and branch, and if the members of that committee did not do so the fault was their own.
The charge has been made that middlemen were employed, but there is no evidence to sustain it. The evidence, on the contrary, shows that the original owner was the only party who had any dealings with the minister. Even with regard to the heating and lighting, to which the hon. gentleman refers as though there was a rake-off, the profit, whatever it was, was made by the proprietor, who wrote to the minister that he was charging only what he paid those who did the heating and lighting.
I.	submit that the ground of this matter could have been better covered by the minister himself than it could possibly be by any other member of this House. Had these charges been made, as they should have been, covering all the various buildings, covering fill the items in respect of which any accusation is made by the opposition, and the minister thus given an opportunity *of meeting them, there would be some satisfaction in our knowing that the gentleman who possessed {ill the knowledge and information with regard to these matters was given a fair and just opportunity to meet these charges. It is easy enough to go into figures. An hon. gentleman who can work out such figures as my hon. friend from Ontario has is wasting his time when he spends it on an investigation by a committee of this House. He ought, instead, to be out in the high financial world engaged in making money. It is easy to take figures and estimate the cost of buildings at a less amount than they are actually worth and then estimate the rental
r.i
cn that estimate and say that what is paid is excessive. It is easy to do this and then point out what a saving would have been effected had the rent been based on a lower value than the proprietor wrould have accepted.

The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-ley), in answering the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), attempted to read into the resolution something which had not been put there by the mover of it. As a mere matter of courtesy, following the usual precedent, the hon. member for Peel had notified the Minister of Public Works that this question would be brought up. And I would say to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Congdon), and to the Minister of Public Works and the members of the government, that this investigation has been before the House and the country since last session, so there can be no complaint on the part of the Minister of Public Works that he has no knowledge, when he was notified by the hon. member for Peel, what matter was to he taken up or what the subject of the amendment would be. But I wish to refer again to the peculiar manner of entering into the debate of the Minister of Public Works. He suggested that the member for Peel had been rather ashamed or afraid of what he had undertaken, and had reduced the percentage rental of these buildings by two percent, and the minister suggested that this was a very serious thing. He did not hesitate to read into the resolution a matter of 25 per cent, and, setting up that straw man in an attempt to deceive the House in the argument he adduced. As the percentage named, was 20 per cent, and not 25 per cent, he attempted to read into the resolution an increase of 25 per cent. In the same way, in arguing the rent per superficial foot of these buildings, the Minister of Public Works does what he -attempted to do before in a similar debate in this House. He referred to the Citizen building, but he did not tell this House that any one going in to rent a room there was paying 90 cents a square foot for the space he occupied and that he got heat, light, repairs, snowcleaning, taxes, insurance and all the expenses in connection with the building, together with the advertising of a large central newspaper building of that kind which in itself is no small matter to any man doing business. These were not figured in in the comparison he made of 81 cents per square foot. That covered the entire building. And not only was he paying 81 cents per foot of the building, basement and attic included, hut, in addition, he was paying for heating, lighting, repairs, and the remov'd of snow'. This was the lease made in regard to the Seybold building. The Minister



of Public Works refused to accept the certified copy of one of the officials of this House, but I have here a printed report of the Public Accounts Committee, printed by the King's Printer, and dated Ottawa, 1910, No. 3. Though the minister refuses to accept a statement certified by one_of the officials, he surely will not refuse to accept the report of one of the committee of this House, printed by the King's Printer. At page 142, I find in a discussion of the very contract we have had before, the House to-night, and on which the arguments of the hon. member for North Ontario were based, the following:-
-The hon. minister has begged the whole question.
-In what way?
-Because you are presupposing that you know this witness is going to say he will not answer the question.
-Not at all.
-Excuse me, now, by your interjection you are intimating to the witness that he need not answer, before you know whether he will object or not.

-Not at all, what I am objecting to is this, and every member of this committee has the right to object to it, to the giving by verbal evidence the contents of a contract which is not produced and which the witness has declined to produce.
Hear, hear.
I will go on to show that the witness was willing to produce the contract had it not been for the attitude of the minister.
Will the hon. gentleman pardon me a moment ?
Order.

I am appealing to the hon. gentleman himself, not to those who are crying ' Order.' But, with the permission of my hon. friend, I will ask him if he does not think that that absolutely corroborates my statement when I say that Mr. Middlebro is seeking to get verbal evidence of the contents of the document? Previous to that time, the document had been produced, and had been taken possession of by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), but the chairman had ruled it out of evidence, and had ordered the hon. member to hand it back. That is the information that was furnished me, and that was why I said before the committee at the time of which he speaks that Mr. Middlebro was trying to get in verbal evidence of the contents of a document.
But the minister said, notwithstanding the evidence as certified by the clerk, that he was not present on that occasion.

I must correct my hon. friend. I made no such statement. I Mr. GOODEVE.
said I was not present when the chairman ruled out the written contract. I came in afterwards and took objection to the attempt to get in secondary evidence of the contract. The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) tried to get in, in a very ingenious way, verbal evidence as to the contents of a contract that had already been ruled out by the chairman.
But the evidence shows that the minister was there from the beginning and remained to the end, for his name appears as voting when the vote was taken.
I may have been there at the end, but not at the beginning.

The minister was present and refused to allow us to hold that contract until we were through with the investigation. That was the whole dispute. We desired that the papers, as in all these investigations, should be freely and frankly laid before this committee and this House. I will show that the minister was there, not as the Minister of Public Works, to assist in making known the facts, but he was there to prevent the witness giving evidence which the witness was prepared to give, and a portion of the committee desired to hear:-[DOT]

-The Minister of Public Works, by taking the stand that he has, is taking the stand that he is the private solicitor for this gentleman who is in the box.
That is exactly what I understood, and I was present.
-How absurd.
-He is, because supposing after you had made this objection, the witness says, ' I do not mind answering at all.'
-That is not proper evidence.

-Then you have no right to interject your objections until you know whether the witness objects to answering or not. You are taking the position of oounsel on this question for the witness.
Hon. Mr. PUGSLEY-The ground I have taken is this-	.

-You have taken it three or four times already.	[DOT]
Yet the hon. minister said on the floor of this House that there was no desire to prevent a free investigation into the questions that were at issue at that time.
And I say so still, but it should be by proper evidence.

-Supposing the witness
says, after you have made that objection, ' I do not mind giving the contents of that document.'
-He might say it, but he has not the right to say that.

-He has the right to say

it if he likes, he is the only man who has the right to say whether he will answer the question or not.
-No, he is not. Will you say that a witness has the right to enter into a dispute here and to be the judge whether he will give by verbal evidence the contents of a written document?
-Are you the judge?
-Yes, and every member of this committee is the judge and the chairman is the judge of that.
-Does this gentleman represent the Woods Company?
-Yes.
-Hasn't he a right to make any admissions he chooses, hasn't he the right to give any evidence he likes if it is true?
-If it is true. I will answer that in a moment.
-Either yes or no, has he the right to give any evidence he likes if it is true?
-You cannot always answer a question with yes or no. Neither this witness or any other witness has the right to give the contents of any document without producing the document.
-Concerning his own company, if it is against his own company.
-No matter who it is against.
-It is against his own company.
-That has nothing to do with it. Because a man says ' I am a fool ' it does not follow that he has any right to say it.
-Do you mean to say that if this man came here and said ' I am getting that electricity for one-half the price I am selling it to the government,' he cannot produce the contract?

-He is not obliged to produce the contract himself.
Yet in face of that evidence we find the Minister of Public Works refusing to allow the witness to give us the necessary information whereby we can learn whether this country is paying unduly through a middleman.
Does my hon. friend deny that long before that the chairman had ruled out the contract and I was objecting to secondary evidence of it?

That was your own opinion, to which other members of the committee took exception. The whole evidence goes to show that it was with the greatest difficulty the opposition members on that committee could get the necessary evidence to prove, as eventually it was proved, that there was a large rake-off through middlemen, in the heating, lighting and using of power in this building. I think my hon. friend from North Ontario has dealt very fully with that question, and he has proved conclusively that an investigation into this question is sadly 74}
needed. Now, there is another building that has been referred to by the Minister of Public Works, and while I am not going to deal with it along the same lines as the other buildings, I want at least to show the care and the interest that the Minister of Public Works has for those with whom he is doing business, and who are on terms of friendship with this government. On coming down to this session I found, when the Auditor General's Report was laid on the table, this letter at page V-356:
Audit Office, March 31, 1910.
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your application No. 991, for $2,500, in favour of the Otis-Fensom Elevator Company, being the cost of installation of one passenger elevator in the Seyhold Block, Ottawa.
The Seybold Block is a building rented by the government for use as the local custom house.
We would like to have a copy of the lease, to see how the cost of this permanent improvement is to be distributed between the landlord and tenant.
I am, sir, your obedient servant, FREDERICK HAYTER, for A.G.
In that letter you will see that the Auditor General refused to issue his check for $2,500, the amount asked for the installation of that elevator. A copy of the lease sent by the office of the Minister of the Public Works contained a clause whereby the lessor was to provide a fully equipped passenger elevator, at the cost, of course, of the lessor: Now what is the answer of the Minister of Public Works and his department?
Public Works Department,
Ottawa, April 28, 1910.
Sir,-Replying to you favour of the 25th instant referring to terms of lease of the Seybold block, relating to elevator, I may say that on the report of the chief architect that the elevator which was in the building when leased had got into a condition incapable of repair and endangered the lives of those making use of it, the department called upon the owner of the building to install a new machine, but could get no reply from him. As an elevator in the building was absolutely essential, the department decided to make the installation and pay for same in the meantime until action was taken by the owner.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,

You will notice there that the only reason given why the Department of Public Works undertook to install an elevator at the public expense, although they had a contract under seal that the lessor was to supply the elevator, was because, he failed to answer when tKey called his attention to the fact that he had not lived up to his contract.
Audit Office,
Ottawa, May 3, 1910.
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of April 28, 1910, respecting the in-

stallation of an elevator in the Seybold block, stating that the department had called upon the owner of the building to install a new machine but could get no reply, and that, as an elevator was essential, the department *decided to make the installation and pay for the same until action was taken by the owner.
As the elevator was installed under agreement with the department, the responsibility for payment to the contractor rests with the government, and with that view assent has been given to the issuance of the check to the Otis-Fenson Elevator Company.
Under the terms of the lease, the owner agrees to supply an elevator fully equipped and ready for use. Please retain from the owner of the Seybold block any sums of money which may become due to him for rental of the said building until the department has been fully reimbursed for all expenses incurred on account of the installation of this elevator.
I am, sir, your obedient servant.

.	For Auditor General.
_ Now, having some experience last year in the Public Accounts Committee, I thought I would like to know whether the order of the Auditor General had been complied with, and whether the rents had been retained to reimburse the government for the installation of this elevator. Therefore 1 put this question on the Order Paper, 'Hansard' page 1333:
Has tbe government been reimbursed for the $2,500 paid by them for the installation of an elevator in the *Seybold building, as per letter of the Auditor General dated May 81, 1910? If so, how and when?.

The Department of Justice now has under consideration the question whether owner or department should pay under the terms of the lease.
A most remarkable state of affairs. Here we have a lease regularly drawn made between the government of Canada and the owner of this building in which h# agrees to install a passenger elevator
And what did he do.
I will show that he did not do it.

Department of Public Works,

The account to be retained from Mr. Seybold is $2,766.29, but I do not understand the order for that retention to be so imperative as to call for immediate action.
We are in actual possession of the building on a long lease, and the rental accruing between the present time and the 31st March Mr. GOODEVE.
next will be more than sufficient to cover the amount.
Under the circumstances, and in view of Mr. Seybold's explanation in conversation with yourself and myself last week, I consider that we might safely pay him the quarter's rent which is now due.
(Sgd.) A. KINGSTON,
Accountant.
We have another letter in connection with that letter, a surprising one, because one is at a loss to know whether the writer, being a lawyer, was retained by the lessor, Mr. Seybold, or whether it is simply as a matter of friendship that he undertakes out of good will to give his advice to this government and tell them what they ought to do under the circumstances.
Ottawa, Sept. 27, 1910. Hon. Wm. Pugsley, D.C.L., P.C., M.P., Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Referring to the conversation which Mr. J. A. Seybold and I bad with you to-day, in reference to the claim which the department has made upon him to pay for the new elevator which was installed by the department in Mr. Seybold's building, which was leased to the government by indenture of lease, dated the 5th day of May, 1908; I beg to state that I can see nothing in the lease which calls upon Mr. Seybold to pay for the installation of a new elevator.
The facts, with regard to the elevator, are shortly these:
The department had this building under lease for the census, and at that time installed a new elevator under the terms of the lease. The lease ran out, and after ah interval of a year or so, a new lease was entered into in 1908, and the clause in the new lease which the department evidently relies on, is as follows : ' The lessor also hereby covenants and agrees to provide in said building an elevator, fully equipped and ready for use, to be operated by the lessee.'
The government took possession of the building on tlie 5th of May, 1908, and for nearly a year, or to be accurate, eleven months, maintained the passenger elevator which was fully equipped and ready for use, as provided for in the lease.
I feel sure that you will agree with me, after a perusal of the lease, that Mr. Seybold cannot be called upon by the government to pay for this new elevator.	,
I have the honour to be, sir,
Yours respectfully, (Sgd.) H. B. MoGIVERIN.
Is that the member of parliament?

The member of parliament. We have after the reception of that letter a remarkable change. We find that evidently he has great influence with the department because we have another letter which is as follows :
Ottawa, 11th October, 1910.
Sir,-I am desired by my minister to refer to you enclosed communication of Mr. Me-

Giverin, M.P., and to ask for legal opinion whether this department is warranted in withholding, under the clause referred to in the lease, from the rent of this building, an amount to cover the cost of putting the elevator in serviceable condition.
I enclose for your information this department's file in the matter, No. 245, in which you will note a letter from me to Mr. J. A. Sey-bold, under date of March 24, 1909, calling on him to install a new machine; also correspondence from the office of the Auditor General in this connection, under date of April 25 and May 3, 1910.
I have the honour to be, sir
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) J. B. HUNTER,
*	Deputy Minister.
The Deputy Minister of Justice,
Ottawa.
Then we have another letter that I would like to read in conjunction with the letter from Mr. McGiverin, and it is from the chief architect :
Chief Architect's Office,
Public Works Department,
November 14, 1910.
J. B. Hunter, Esq.,
Deputy Minister,
Public Works Department.
I am returning correspondence re elevator in Seybold building. In reference to the question of the deputy Minister of Justice, ' I have to ask therefore whether the lessor provided at the time you entered into possession of the property under lease, an elevator fully equipped and ready for use.'
When the department first rented the building for Census Branch, the elevator was a freight elevator, and the lessor changed it to a passenger elevator, but it never gave satisfaction. When the building was re-leased in May, 1908, for customs purposes, the same elevator was in it, and the long room being on the second floor, the elevator was in constant use by the public, but it did not give satisfaction and was continuously requiring repairs, which were made by and at the expense of this department. Complaints were so frequent that the elevator was examined by our chief electrician, and he reported that the mechanism was beyond repair, and the elevator was dangerous. New mechanism has been put in and the elevator is now in good condition.
(Sgd.) D. EWART,
Chief Architect.
Now, after reading these letters in connection with the lease, there is only one inference to be drawn, and not an inference, as_ the letters themselves actually prove this condition. It is that the building was formerly leased to the Dominion government for census purposes. At that time there was in the building a freight elevator. There seems to be some confu->V5^.-^e*'^veen the chief architect, and Mr. McGiverin as to who altered it into a passenger elevator, the one stating that it was done at the expense of the lessor, and the other stating that it was done at the
expense of the lessee. In either case it was evidently unsatisfactory. That is admitted by both letters, but it is further proven by the fact that when the government undertook to renew the lease of this building they specifically set forth in the lease, notwithstanding the fact that they knew that there was already an old elevator in the building that the lessor should instal a passenger elevator ready for use. Why? There can be only one answer-because, having used the building before and knowing that there was already an elevator, they also knew that the elevator was dangerous, that it was unsatisfactory, and for that reason they -put a clause in the lease stipulating that the lessor should furnish the government with a passenger elevator fully equipped and, of course, inspected that it might be used under the laws of the country for passengers. The government went in and took possession, and notwithstanding that they had that document, we find the deputy minister saying that because he wrote to the owner of the building and received no answer he felt that it was his duty to order the installation of a new public passenger elevator at the expense of the people of this country. I find in the Auditor General's Report in connection with that elevator that they paid out $3,031.18 although their lease called for the installation of it by the lessor. The minister objected to the resolution on the ground that they were only paying from 7 to 10 per cent in rental, and yet we find in this one case alone, certified to by the Auditor General, certified to by the chief architect, and the deputy minister of his department, that they voluntarily expended $3,031 or an amount equal to 47 per cent of the rental for one year for an elevator in ia building that they had no right to pay for. Even in the Auditor General's Report it distinctly states that they had no right to pay it, and the deputy minister states himself in his letter that they were only paying this in the meantime because they feared the danger of the old elevator that had been condemned. Then we find them endeavouring to shelve this problem, as they shelve other problems, by saying that they had referred it to the Department of Justice. This is another instance of carelessness in the handling of the funds of the people of this country. I think we are not using too strong language when we speak of rake-offs of this kind. I have put in a question, and I hope to receive through the Public Acounts Committee the total amount which has been expended toy this government in alterations, repairs and capital expenditures on this building. I was in hopes that I would have had these returns before this question came up in the House, but we will probably find it necessary to

deal with the question later on when we get all these details. In the meantime I want at least to enter my protest against the manner in which the administration of the department with regard to these rented buildings is carried on.
