speechtext:
The observations of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Goodeve), who has just taken his seat do not call for any strenuous reply from the government side of the- House. He has given us some history in connection with the elevator, which history does not reflect the slightest discredit on the administration of the Public Works department. It turns out that a certain elevator used for passengers in one of these buildings is found to be in a defective condition and that human life might be jeopardized. The deputy minister in compliance with the authority which the lease gave him, called on the proprietor of the building to put the elevator ip good condition according to the terms of the lease as he understood them. The moment the deputy minister did that, he put himself in a position to charge the cost of that elevator against the proprietor of the building, should he refuse to take action, and if the government are entitled under the lease to do so, they can deduct the cost of that elevator out of the rental. The deputy minister of Public Works was charged with the responsibility of seeing that the elevator was safe, and would any sensible man suggest that instead of taking immediate action, he should go into a court of law to get a mandamus or injunction against the owner of the building, when in the meantime, those using the elevator might be killed. Had an accident happened, would it avail the deputy minister of Public Works to say that in order to avoid the criticism of members of the opposition and to save a few paltry dollars, he had delayed action in making the elevator safe for the use of passengers. The elevator story therefore may be eliminated from a consideration of the case for it affords no proof whatever that there was any remissness on the part of the government; on the contrary, the action which was taken reflects credit on the department. It is a matter of common occurrence that there is difference of opinion between landlords and lessees as to the construction of an agreement, and pending a settlement of that dispute before a proper tribunal the deputy minister of Public Works removed the cause of danger as any honest conscientious man would do. Surely it is time enough to blame the government when they are found to be in fault, and pending a decision on this point is it not at least decent, to withhold criticism. So far as I could learn from the hon. member for Kootenay Mr. GOODEVE.
(Mr. Goodeve), the case with regard to the elevator is still sub judice, and as I understand my hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) is a lawyer, he will know well that the etiquette of the profession forbids him to come here and make a speech and discuss the evidence in a case which has yet to be dealt with by . the courts. I understand the hon. gentleman to be a lawyer and a good and experienced one, and I would expect him to leave this evidence alone until we have had a final decision in regard to the matter. I appeal to the members of this House as jurors who have to deal with the amendment presented by the hon. member for Peel to say that no evidence has been submitted in support of his indictment. The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve), tried to make a great point out of the part the Minister of Public Works took in the inquiry before the Public Accounts Committee, and I regret that hon. members of the opposition who sit on that committee are continuously complaining without reason, upon the alleged obstructions that are thrown in their way. I have been a member of that committee for some years and I challenge any hon. member of this House to say that I have objected to any honest or proper inquiry that ever took place there. I am in the hearing of hon. gentlemen who sit with me on that committee and I challenge them to say that I ever unduly obstructed any proper inquiry. I speak, of -course, only for myself, but l think I may be taken ,as perhaps a very ordinary sample of the Liberals who sit with me on that very important committee. I do not refer to what may have happened in years past when I was no-t a member of the committee, but my experience leads me to conclude that the practices then were not very different from what they are to-day. Hon. gentlemen opposite are making a great mistake if they think the people of this country will take much stock in this howling about obstruction unless they can produce more substantial proof of it, than they yet have been able to. I followed with some interest and concern the inquiry before the committee, and I give credit to the hon. member for North-Ontario for having pursued this question with a great deal of energy and industry, but he only made one point before -the committee and in that he was sustained by the Liberals as well as by the Conservatives. It came out in the inquiry that the department was imposed upon with regard to the lighting and that practically a fraud was being committed from day to day and from month to month. I do not know how long it lasted, but it came out flatfooted that fraud was being committed, and we all joined hands in passing a resolution that that wrongdoing should at once cease and that if there had been any money im-

properly received, it should be' paid back. I voted against every other resolution moved by the hon. member (Mr. Sharpe), at the close of the inquiry, because I did not think he had sustained the allegations he had made, I do not think he sustained the allegations he made about the heating or about the venting and I am still of the same opinion rafter hearing the evidence rehashed to-night. Speaking in a general way, I submit that the government of the country is in no different position to an individual, when they go into the market to rent buildings. They have no business to look for cheaper rentals than any other man. True, the ordinary man would not require such large buildings, and therefore the buildings required by the government are naturally few, in a city of this kind, and you consequently would expect to find the rentals for such buildings higher than for ordinary buildings.
Gentlemen of my own profession know that law books are dearer than other kinds of books, because there is only a limited market for them. Doctors, I suppose, have a similar experience. The class of buildings the government require in the city of Ottawa are a special class, different from any other kind of buildings, and for different purposes. Therefore, the supply is limited, apd those who have the supply can afford to put the price at a pretty steep figure. I suppose they know that and take advantage of it. All I wanted to know at the committee was whether the government was paying as much as others in the way of rental, no more and no less. I made that inquiry, and having satisfied myself that they werg^not paying more than the humblest individual in Ottawa who had to rent a building, I was content that the government should pay the same as other people, and therefore voted against the resolution of the hon. member for North Ontario. I am satisfied that there was not a scintilla of evidence given in support of the indictment of the hon. member for Peel. It was shown that we were paying 81 cents per superficial foot, or 90 cents, as the case might be. Is there any evidence that we could have got the accommodation for any less? If it can be shown th^t by the exercise of due diligence the department could have obtained a superficial area to suit the purposes of the government for one cent less they are to be condemned for not obtaining it. But when there is not a scintilla of evidence to show that they could have done any better than was clone, what is the use. of indicting them? They paid the price which the market demanded, and they could not get it lowered. I submit that there is not a particle of evidence of wrong-doing. Even if the rental was a little high, if the members of the government, and particularly the
department under consideration to-night, exercised the best judgment they possessed in the interests of the.people of this country, and gave the people the benefit of their judgment, honestly and squarely, are they to be indicted or condemned for having paid a cent per superficial foot one way or the other in renting buildings of the magnitude of those they have to deal with?
Does not my hon. friend think 18 per cent a little high?

There is not a particle of evidence that there is 18 per cent. My hon. friend from Peel has given us what is known in Scotland as a Scotch trial-he first hangs the accused and then tries him. The hon. gentleman asks for a verdict and he tells the jury: I have no evidence; I am putting the facts as I have them, and some time next week I will give you the evidence. Although not a lawyer, my hon. friend is not without experience and strong common sense, and he is one of the men who give tone and respectability to the opposition side of the House, and yet I must charge him with having a very crude idea of how cases should be tried.

May 1 ask my hon. friend whether he disputes the facts I presented to the House this afternoon with respect to the purchase price of the property and the amount expended on it, to make the cost of it $80,000 in all to the present owners?

I certainly cannot accept such evidence when we know nothing about it. I am not saying that my hon. friend's statements may not turn out to be correct, but so far they are not facts at all. There is no evidence before us, and we are bound in all fairness to deal with the Minister of Public Works upon the evidence submitted to us. He is charged with all manner of political crimes in connection with the leasing of these buildings, and surely he has a right as a minister of the Crown to ask his supporters and every honest man in this House to condemn him on facts, and not upon the bald statements which my hon. friend may make, however honestly he may make them. My hon. friend was asked to disclose the source of his alleged facts, but he refused to do so, telling us that some day in the Committee of Public Accounts he would give us those facts.
It is altogether unnecessary for me to go over any of the ground that was traversed by the Minister of Public Works himself. The answer he gave to the allegations contained in the indictment of the hon. member for Peel was so complete that there is nothing left for the jury even to pass upon As the old saying is, there is nothing of it left to be buried. There have been many insinuations of bad faith and what hon. gentlemen of the opposition call rake-off

in connection with these matters. With regard to the electric light contract, is there, a particle oi evidence that there was any laxity or any wrong-doing in connection with it so far as the minister or any of the officials of the department is concerned? I think it quite proper that there should be further inquiry into that matter. I have seen the papers, and I am surprised that any official of the city of Ottawa should be allowed to be a party to a transaction of that kind. Whether wittingly or not, the city of Ottawa has become a party to a dishonest transaction in enabling certain individuals or firms to obtain money to which they have no right, and I hope the Department of Public Works will, before long, be able to tell us that proper steps have been taken to recover any moneys that have improperly gone out in that way.
When insinuations of this kind are made one is almost tempted to go back and to see whence came those men who are so very honest, what are their names, and what was their former occupation. I do not like it, and it is not according to my idea of public duty or public business to go into muck-raking of any kind. I ask the hon. member for Peel, when he goes home to-night, to think over the last 30 or 40 years, and to inquire how the public works of this country were built and what is become of certain public inquiries at certain stages of this country's political history. Having done that, if lie thinks he can come forth and be the first to throw stones from a political standpoint I shall be willing to follow out some of the points he. has endeavoured to make against us to-night, but I am satisfied that, from every standpoint, the arraignment he has endeavoured to make is completely unfounded, and that if this matter came before a judge in any court he would withdraw the charges from the jury and say that there was nothing left on which to found a verdict.

The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has spoken about the elevator in the Seybold block and he was quite right in saying that an elevator was necessary there because human lives were in jeopardy and that the department could charge the proprietor with the cost. But unfortunately it did not charge the proprietor with the cost, and consequently did not do what the hon. gentleman said it should have done. It is hardly necessary for me to comment on the hon. gentleman's remarks with reference to the Regal building because he says no evidence was given by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) with regard to that matter, if the hon. member for Cape Breton is willing to swallow that 18 per cent rent, his capacity in that respect is unusually strong.
Mr. MeKENZIE.
There is no proof whatever that it is 18 per cent or even 10 per cent except the hearsay statement of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain).

What strikes me as the worst feature in this transaction is the business inefficiency it has shown on the part of the Department of Public Works. The minister says that they take great care in the making of these leases. Well, they certainly take great care to pay too much. I listened with much attention to the hon. member for Peel with regard to this Regal building. As respects the other buildings I have very little knowledge, but I know a good deal about the Regal building and property in the vicinity, and in my opinion my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) showed conclusively that the government was paying 18 per cent to the owners. I have no fault to find with the proprietors for having got all they could-it was a business transaction, but I have fault to find with the department for having been so unbusinesslike as to give this enormous rental. The hon. minister said there is no proof of that. Why, that the exact cost of the building was $47,500 is a matter oi public knowledge, can be seen in the registry office. All they did afterwards was to add another story or two to the building, and when completed I am safe in saying that $80,000 would be a full market price for it in this city. The minister has tried to cloud the issue by talking about rents by the square foot for other buildings rented by this government. That is a most unfair way in which to discuss the question. When I rent an office in a building by the square foot, I get the use of the elevator free, pay nothing for the hallways and as a rule get the use of the light and have the heating without charge. But in this Regal building, the government is doing all these things. All the proprietors have to pay out of their rent is the insurance.

Does the hon. gentleman say that in the figure I gave of 81 -28 per square foot, I have included the hallway? Take the Regal building and all the buildings, the figures given are for the portions actually occupied for offices and do not include anything except the actual office space.

I still say, and I submit to the minister, that the proper way to judge this rental is to compare it with the rental of other buildings rented as a whole, and not take it by the square foot at all. Every one knows that in Ottawa, as in other places, a man who buys property in the heart of the city is very glad to rent the whole building to net him 5 per cent or 6 per cent per annum, because he gets the increased value which comes regularly and steadily in all these cities. I happen to

know from personal knowledge of a lease of property behind this Regal building, slightly larger than the Regal building, and it is on Sparks street, and for that reason worth a great deal more, and it has been rented for $7,000 per annum within the last few days, and out of that the owner has to pay the insurance.
What building?
The Bryson, Graham building.
How large?
Slightly larger than this.
How many stories?

Three or four, immediately behind and in a much more valuable part than the Regal building. I did not intend to speak on this motion, but rose to make tliat statement. I consider that it is only right and nroper that the lease of the Regal building should be compared with a building rented as a whole, and it is not good business capacity on the part of this government to pay over $14,000 per annum net to the owners of the Regal building when other people are able to rent buildings in Ottawa of greater value for half the money.

With reference to leases, it is hard to make comparisons, but the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has said that some of these buildings were rented to net the proprietor from 18 per cent to 25 per cent. Now there are many towns in which commercial buildings are renting to pay more than that on the actual investment though perhaps not on the actual value. Values are continually changing. I know' properties in Toronto that have been rented as high as 80 per cent on the cost, but still would not bring more than 7 per cent on the actual value, considering the value of the land and the value of the building, and so far as I have been able to judge with reference to departmental buildings here, they have nearly all to be constructed almost specially for the purpose of the departments. Take the building just mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) which he compares with the one leased hy the government. The probabilities are that the building he mentioned was rented_ as it was without any particularly extensive repairs. And the probabilities are that the building rented to the department required extensive repairs in the way of elevators and other improvements for the department.
Now, these extensive inside repairs would cost a good deal of money. My hon. friend says they only added a couple of stories. Well, a couple of stories properly added to the building, with the repairs necessary to fit the building for occupation by a department of the government, might cost a great deal of money, and it is perfectly fair to add the actual cost. Suppose they bought the building for $47,000, and expended $25,000-say $75,000 altogether. They might have so improved that building as to make it worth $50,000 more in the eyes of any real estate valuator. It is a common practice among real estate valuators to take the gross rental at 10 per cent in order to pay the investor 6 per cent net on his money. The building must be in very excellent condition in which a gross 10 per cent will net the owner 6 per cent by the time he pays his ordinary wear and tear repairs. Now, as to the Canadian building and the others that were inquired into so much in the Committee of Public Accounts: I was in the committee a good deal of the time, and when the Minister of Public Works says that when the question was raised that the chairman ruled out of order, he was not there, I believe he is absolutely right. The vote was taken on a question of sustaining the chairman's decision.
And the report shows it.

The members on our side did not dispute the right of members on the other side to inquire into this question, and to compare the cost of lighting and heating with that in any other buildings of a similar size in town, or to get the cost of lighting and heating-of lighting more especially-from the electrical department of the city." But I remember saying that they had no' right to inquire into the private agreement between the Realty Company and the lighting department. I said, and I still say, that that was beyond what we had the right to inquire into. I thought these hon. gentlemen had every right to compare the cost of lighting and heating with that of similar buildings elsewhere in the city. Now, as a matter of fact, when the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and others proved that these people were getting what he calls a rake-off, that is, getting a profit' out of the light, we immediately joined with them and the Minister of Public Works cancelled the contract. It appears that the contract was made many years ago when the government were using only a part of the building, and, for the sake of convenience, the owner agreed to light the part used by the government at the same proportionate cost that he was paying. They did not suspect him, I suppose; in any event, they did not know-at least, I do not think they knew-that they were paying more for the lighting than he was paying. It turned out by the evidence before the committee, that, apparently, they were, and the contract was immediately cancelled.

I was not a member of this committee, and perhaps I may be allowed a question for information. I thought the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt)
. said that he was opposed to inquiring into what the Realty Company had paid for the lighting?
I said that was a private contract.
How would the hon. gentleman have found out about the rake-off?
It was simply the case so far as that is concerned.
But if you were not at liberty to inquire into it, how could you ever correct' it, suppose that an unjust amount were charged to the government?
We took it in comparison with what we knew of the cost of other buildings.

I am asking for information. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the committee ought not to have inquired into what the Realty Company were paying. But if they did not get it in that way, they would not have saved the country three or four thousand dollars.
They did not get at it that way; they guessed at it.

If I may be allowed: up to the very close of the inquiry it appeared as if Mr. Woods had had some old contract with the city and that the department had simply paid to the Imperial Realty Company the bills which had been rendered to it. But, towards the close of the inquiry, I learned that the city, through the electrical department, presided over by Mr. Ellis, the treasurer of the city, had, quarter after quarter, rendered accounts charging the Imperial Realty Company with the quantity of electrical current at meter rate which were turned in by the Imperial Realty 'Company to the government and charged against the department, these accounts rendered by the municipal electrical department to the Imperial Realty Company being marked settled by the municipal department of the city and sent in to my department as vouchers. The momejit that appeared, I instructed the deputy minister to say that we would take steps to cancel the contract and to recover the excess money paid by the department under these circumstances. The committee did not further investigate the matter," but the resolution was passed unanimously. I took the necessary steps by communicating with the city and demanding an account of
what the Realty Company had really paid to the city and sent the matter to the Department of Justice. That is the way it finally wound up.

I understood that, owing to the opposition to the heating contract, that also was cancelled. I understand, however, that the heating would cost more this year than it did under the contract; and, so far as I can find out, there will not be a saving to the country owing to the government doing its own heating. And you can easily understand that any private party could get this heating done by keeping the men working longer hours- you know the agitation that constantly arises here for shorter hours for government employees. Hon. members can judge of the matter for themselves, but, I understand, as a matter of fact, that the heating this year will be more expensive than under the old contract. As to the lighting, we do not know yet, but I question ser-| iously if there will be so much saved on, the lighting contract as was supposed to be saved when we cancelled the contract. We shall know at the end of the year, no doubt, how much will be saved, i understand there is a flat rate, and, if there is, there may be a considerable saving on the lighting contract.
The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) made quite a fuss over putting in an elevator. I quite agree that the government did exactly what any sensible business man would do in his own interest under similar circumstances. Rather than run the risk of actions by the employees, they put in a new elevator, and they purposed taking it off the rent, judging by the deputy minister's letter. But I suppose this lessor objected very seriously to them doing that; so the government, instead of jumping into a lawsuit, which is easily done by any government, and generally getting the worst of it, referred the question to the Justice Department. Now what else would they do, as sensible men? I think they did perfectly right in that respect. There was one little thing that I thought entirely uncalled for on the part of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), and I may say that I was very much surprised to hear him say it. He might have said it in the heat of debate, but all the same, it was a nasty little stab. He said that the hon. the Minister of Public Works was living at the Roxborough apartments, and that the hon. member for Car-leton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) was also living at the Roxborough apartments. Now as a matter of fact I know that the Minister of Public Works, when these agreements were cancelled, and during all the time they were in force, was living at the Aylmer apartments, because I was living there myself. It was-after then that he went to the Roxborough apartments, this fall, after they

were finished. My hon. friend smiles, he is very suspicious. 'Evil be to him that evil thinks' is an old proverb that you probably all know. Now I am not so suspicious of other people as he is; and 1 repeat, that was a nasty, dirty little stab, to say about the Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Carleton, absolutely uncalled for, because it was made in such a way that it could not be got at. I was very much surprised to hear it.
Now I want to say a word with reference to this Public Accounts Committee. I go to the Public Accounts Committee, frequently, and I have heard so many suspicions voiced at it, so many insinuations- made against, it, such a hue and cry about what was going on in this committee, that I have become disgusted. There never was really anything proved to justify it. They bring witnesses there from all over Canada; it must cost something, I do not know who pays for this evidence. These men come from all over Canada, and you find there a half dozen gentlemen questioning them as if they were thieves. Why, if you were to go into an ordinary court of justice the judge would not allow witnesses to be badgered, and questioned, and subjected to all sorts of insinuations. It reminds me of an ordinary division court where there are a lot of cheap lawyers trying to plug some poor devil that owes a dollar. Now we do not try to oppose these gentlemen in ordinary reason and common sense, but they don't allow the witnesses fair play. I always like to see fair play anywhere. I don't like to see half a dozen men pile on to one poor innocent fellow, that is likely scared to death when he is in the Public Accounts Committee.
What about the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee?
The chairman of the committee is a gentleman, and he treats everybody on that committee as gentlemen.	'
Does he not defend the witness?

Why, if he did, they would rag at the chairman worse than they do at the witness. The only thing that I can see for the w-itness to do is just to tell these gentlemen: Go to some-where else. But there seems to be no ordinary reasonable usage accorded a witness, especially if he happens to be a little timid when he gets up in the Public Accounts Committee; and then my hon. friend from Carleton generally steps in and tries to protect him a little, and perhaps somebody else steps in. Then our friends opposite say that he is obstructing the work of the committee. Now, I remember distinctly when that examination was going on, and I am quite sure the Minister of Public Works was just as polite as any man could
be to the members of the committee. He only tried to observe ordinary decency towards the witness, and only to that extent did he try to protect him. Now hon. members on that committee, so far as I could judge, as a spectator, at least, were really nagging the witness unnecessarily, they were trying to put words into his mouth, just as is often done in some little country court. The lawyers on that committee are trying to get from the witness just such an answer as they want: Answer'that question I put to you, yes or no. They don't give the poor fellow any opportunity to answer the question in a reasonable way, and many a question cannot be answered yes or no, and answered reasonably. Now I can tell our hon. friends opposite that if they will be reasonable, we will assist them in every possible way to investigate any question in the Public Accounts Committee; because I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we are just as much interested as they are in seeing the affairs of this country carried on economically and properly.
I hardly think so.
Has the hon. gentleman ever seen me give any indication that I was not willing and anxious to see the affairs of this country conducted properly and honestly?

The hon. member is asking me a question. Personally, I have not seen him raise objections which I thought were wrong, because I have not been on the committee much lately; I am not on the committee. But over and over again, I have seen hon. members supporting the government on that committee interpose what I consider absolute obstruction for the purpose of preventing information coming out.

Well, it is like everything else in the world, it depends largely on how you look at it, on the point of view, as it were. I suppose the hon. gentleman means my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., when he speaks of obstruction. Now, I have never seen my hon. friend from Carleton, unreasonable, unless the members of the opposition were attacking a witness unreasonably. _ I believe the member for Carleton, is just as anxious to see the affairs of this country conducted economically as anybody else in this House, I have always thought so, and I still think so. Now, as to the rentals paid for these various buildings by the Public Works Department. I cannot conceive that the Department of Public Works are anxious to pay these gentlemen more for their buildings than they can make out of them in other uses. You must bear in mind the peculiar position the department is in. They must have a building fit

for their purpose. It is all right for lion, members to say that the government might go on and erect a building. So they could, but there is always such a hue and cry all the time about expenses, that the department finds it better in many instances to rent these buildings instead of buying them. For instance, take that building that is earning, as they say, 18 per cent. It would not pay the government to buy that building, it is not suited for their purpose even with the repairs. It is riot the sort of building the government would put up for an office building. Therefore, they would have been shortsighted in my judgment to have bought the building. I believe that the government will, as soon as they reasonably can, erect a building to accommodate all the departments. It is a great pity that there was not sufficient foresight many years ago to retain the land around where these buildings are, so as to provide sites for all the public buildings in this vicinity. But, the government had to do the best they could to provide accommodation for the department. With reference to the calculation made by the hon. member for North Ontario, I quite agree with the hon. member for the Yukon, that the hon. gentleman is wasting his time in this House. There are many concerns in the world that, I venture to say, would give him $50,000 a year if he could float corporations and bonds in the same way as he calculated the government ought to float them. He assumed that the building would cost $650,000 and he said that there was no trouble to get a mortgage on that for $500,000. I would like to see my hon. friend go out and get it.
Bo the government guarantee it?
For how long?
Ten years.
Part of it for five years and part for ten years. What would that do? I would like to see my hon. friend take these bonds anywhere and try to float them.
In ten years the total rental would amount to $683,141.
What about the repairs and interest on the money?
The government were doing the repairs.

That brings me to this point: The government did the repairs when they found it was absolutely necessary to get the lease. They did not agree to do the repairs in connection with the first lease. They had to undertake to do the repairs in order to get the second lease, just as any one in this House would do if Mr. NESBITT.
he were forced. They had to do it and we have not the slightest doubt that the government did the best they could in the interest of the country in renting these buildings and that they did not pay one dollar more for repairs than they were forced to pay by reason of their having to secure accommodation.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Public Works has invoked the sympathy of the House, and it has been invoked on his behalf by other hon. gentlemen for the reason that the minister has not the opportunity of making a reply to the very forcible observations of my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe). My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is too old a parliamentarian not to know that he could have asked any one of his friends who have spoken here this evening to move the adjournment of the debate and enable him to answer my hon. friend from North Ontario if he had any answer to make. He knows that perfectly well, and he cannot deny it now. Therefore, it was rather idle to appeal to the sympathy of the House on that account when he might, in five minutes, by asking one of his colleagues to move the adjournment of the debate, have obtained the right to make any answer that he saw fit. Further than that, in so far as I am concerned, I will not object to his making any answer that he has to make at this moment to my hon. friend from North Ontario.
I thank my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) for his courtesy, and after the other hon. gentlemen get through I will make a general answer to what has oeen said.

No, my hon. friend can take the alternative; he may move the adjournment of the debate, or so far as I am concerned I have no objection at all to his answering my hon. friend from North Ontario at once; but I hope he will extend the same courtesy to some hon. gentleman on this side of the House.

The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) opened the debate by simply confining his attention to .one building out of a number. I followed my hon. friend and not knowing then what would be said with reference to other buildings I did refer to them. Now, then, it seems to me that a fair way to do would be that after other hon. gentlemen get through I may be allowed to reply.
Oh, no.
Is the hon. gentleman afraid to allow me to reply?

I am not afraid of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) in any way,
2.345

but I want to have a fair understanding. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) offers to allow the hon. minister an opportunity to speak no w if he thinks fit, and that is a very great concession. The minister knew perfectly well the line of argument that was going to be taken. This is a revote to make provision for the procuring and installation of new boilers, a new smoke stack and increasing the height of the chimney at the government printing bureau. The total estimated cost is $11,000.
Why does the minister only ask for $10,000, when the estimated cost is $11,000 ?
I expect that the chief architect expects to spend $1,000 before the 31st March. He can do that out of the vote for the current y^ar and allow the other $9,000 to lapse.
We are voting $10,000 for this year ?
Yes. These boilers are very much needed.
Are these to replace old boilers ?
Yes.
We voted a similar amount last year for the same purpose. If it was needed, why was it not spent ?
The only answer I can give is that it was felt possibly that we might put off the work for another year.
Have tenders been called or will they be called for these boilers ?
They have not been yet.
I understand that it is the intention of the government to erect a new printing bureau. Is that a fact ?

There has been some talk of it, I think that my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Murpihy), has the
matter under consideration, but even if that were done, it wmuld be necessary to keep the, present building in an efficient and safe condition, because the new' building would take considerable time to erect.

This has the same defect which many of these items indicate; that it is voted year after year. It could not have been urgently required last year or otherwise I assume it would have been spent. The fact that it was voted la3t year and not spent, is evidence that it is not wanted. We have it this year again, and we do not know but what the same thing may occur next year. [DOT] It is a small amount, but we find the same thing with regard to other public works, such as harbours, rivers and public buildings. I do not think that it indicates good business management, because jf it is urgently needed and we vote the money, it "ought to be spent and if it is not needed, it should not be in the estimates.
Knowing something about machinery, I cannot help wondering how it is that the boilers are all played out at once, and that it is absolutely necessary to put in $10,000 worth of boilers.
The chief architect tells me that the boilers which are now there, were put in when the building was erected many years ago.
At what cost ?

The contract for the construction of the building w'as made in 1887, .and the boilers which are in the building were put there at that time. The chief architect says that the four boilers require replacing. They are getting in pretty bad condition, and the reason that new boilers have not 'been put in during the present year is that the chief architect let the matter run on supposing that the old ones would do for a year longer, but he now feels that they must he replaced.
WTiat is the capacity of the boilers?
The chief architect cannot say without making inquiries as to the horse-power.
Could the minister tell us what the old boilers cost?
No, I presume that they were put in as a part of the contract for the building away back in 1887. No doubt 'by looking up the old accounts the cost could 'be easily arrived at.
That amounts to something about boilers. I cannot help feeling that $10,000 for four boilers bricked is an enormous sum to pay.
